108256.e: Laxatives make poo softer or stimulate the gut. They should only be taken for a short time and on medical advice.
108256.m: Laxatives help with constipation but are not for everyday use.

108257.q: How does exercise help against constipation?
a: It slows the flow of bile
108257.e: Physical activity such as running or cycling gets the gut moving too. People who sit a lot are more likely to get constipated.
108257.m: Exercise gets the gut moving too.

108258.q: From when do people usually speak of constipation in adults?
a: Going for a poo less than 3 times a week
Going for a poo once a day
Going for a poo twice a day
Going for a poo every morning
108258.e: Anything from about three times a day to three times a week is healthy. Less often than three times a week usually counts as constipation.
108258.m: Going for a poo less than three times a week counts as constipation.

108259.q: Why can it lead to constipation if you often hold in the urge to poo?
a: The urge gets weaker over time
108259.e: If you often hold in the urge, the gut gets used to it. The signal gets weaker and the poo stays in the gut for longer.
108259.m: You should go to the toilet soon after you feel the urge.

108260.q: Which foods contain a lot of fibre?
108260.e: Fibre is found in wholegrain products, vegetables, pulses and fruit. Animal foods contain almost none.
108260.m: Wholegrains, vegetables and fruit provide lots of fibre.

108261.q: What is the biggest danger with severe diarrhoea, especially for young children?
108261.e: With diarrhoea, the body loses a lot of water and salts. Young children can become dehydrated quickly.
108261.m: With diarrhoea, the body risks drying out.

108262.q: What should you do above all when you have diarrhoea?
a: Drink plenty, with a little salt and sugar
Drink nothing at all if possible
108262.e: It is important to replace water and salts. Special rehydration drinks from the chemist contain salts and sugar in the right proportions.
108262.m: With diarrhoea, you must replace lost fluid.

108263.q: Which virus often causes contagious vomiting and diarrhoea, especially in winter?
108263.e: Noroviruses are very contagious and suddenly cause vomiting and diarrhoea. Outbreaks often happen in schools, hospitals and on ships.
108263.m: Noroviruses cause contagious vomiting and diarrhoea.

108264.q: Why should you wash your hands especially thoroughly when you have diarrhoea?
a: So you do not pass the germs on
108264.e: Many germs that cause diarrhoea are very contagious and get onto door handles and food via the hands. Washing your hands with soap breaks this path.
108264.m: Hand washing protects others from diarrhoea germs.

108265.q: What is the best way to protect yourself from contagious diarrhoea germs?
108265.e: Many diarrhoea germs are passed on by dirty hands. Washing your hands with soap after the toilet and before eating protects you well.
108265.m: Washing your hands with soap protects against diarrhoea germs.

108266.q: What is the diarrhoea called that people often get in faraway countries from contaminated food or water?
108266.e: Traveller's diarrhoea is the most common illness on trips to hot countries. It is usually caused by bacteria in water or food.
108266.m: Traveller's diarrhoea often comes from contaminated water or food.

108267.q: According to the World Health Organization, from when is it called diarrhoea?
a: Runny poo at least 3 times a day
108267.e: The WHO defines diarrhoea as three or more watery stools a day. So both how often and how runny it is matter.
108267.m: Runny poo three times a day counts as diarrhoea.

108268.q: Which rule of thumb applies to eating in countries with unsafe drinking water?
a: “Boil it, peel it or forget it”
108268.e: Boiling kills germs, and peeling removes the dirty skin. Raw, unpeeled food and ice cubes are risky.
108268.m: When travelling, it is better to skip anything you cannot cook or peel.

a: Stomach acid flows into the oesophagus
Too little saliva in the mouth
108269.e: In heartburn, acidic stomach contents flow back into the oesophagus. Its lining is not protected against acid and burns.
108269.m: Heartburn is caused by stomach acid in the oesophagus.

108270.q: Where do you typically feel heartburn?
108270.e: The burning rises behind the breastbone, sometimes up into the throat. That is where the oesophagus runs.

108271.q: Which muscle normally stops stomach contents from flowing back into the oesophagus?
108271.e: Where the oesophagus joins the stomach there is a sphincter muscle. If it does not close properly, acid can rise up.
108271.m: A sphincter muscle separates the oesophagus and the stomach.

a: Lying down after a big meal
Going for a walk after eating
108272.e: If you lie down with a full stomach, you make it easier for the acid to rise. Big meals also increase the pressure in the stomach.
108272.m: After a big meal, you should not lie down straight away.

108273.q: How do antacids work against heartburn?
108273.e: Antacids contain alkaline substances. These neutralise some of the stomach acid.
108273.m: Antacids make stomach acid less harmful.

108274.q: What is the medical name for stomach contents flowing back into the oesophagus?
108274.e: Reflux comes from the Latin word for flowing back. If it happens often, it is called reflux disease.
108274.m: Stomach contents flowing back is called reflux.

108275.e: Fatty food stays in the stomach for a long time and can loosen the sphincter to the oesophagus. Spicy food, coffee and chocolate can also cause problems.
108275.m: Very fatty food can trigger heartburn.

108276.q: Why does raising the upper body in bed help against heartburn at night?
a: The stomach then makes no acid
108276.e: If the upper body is higher, the acid has to rise against gravity. It manages this much less well.
108276.m: A raised upper body makes it harder for acid to rise.

108277.q: Which acid is in stomach acid?
108277.e: The stomach lining makes hydrochloric acid. It makes the gastric juice strongly acidic.

108278.q: Roughly what pH does the gastric juice in an empty stomach have?
108278.e: With a pH of about 1 to 2, the empty stomach is very acidic. A pH of 7 would be neutral.

108279.q: Which cells in the stomach lining make the acid?
108279.e: The parietal cells sit in the glands of the stomach lining. They release the acid into the inside of the stomach.

108280.q: What protective job does stomach acid do?
108280.e: Many bacteria and other germs do not survive the strong acid. In this way the stomach protects against germs in food.
108280.m: Stomach acid kills many germs in food.

108281.q: Why does stomach acid not digest the stomach wall itself?
a: A layer of mucus protects it
The stomach is made of bone
The stomach wall is made of fat
108281.e: The stomach lining makes a thick layer of mucus. It keeps the acid away from the cells.
108281.m: Mucus protects the stomach wall from its own acid.

108282.q: Which protein-splitting enzyme is activated by stomach acid?
108282.e: The stomach releases an inactive form called pepsinogen. The acid turns it into the active enzyme pepsin.
108282.m: Stomach acid activates the enzyme pepsin.

108283.q: Roughly how much gastric juice does an adult make each day?
108283.e: The stomach lining makes about 2 to 3 litres of gastric juice every day. It contains acid, mucus and enzymes.
108283.m: The stomach makes several litres of gastric juice every day.

108284.q: What does stomach acid do to the proteins in food?
108284.e: The acid destroys the shape of the proteins; they are denatured. Unfolded proteins are easier for enzymes to break down.
108284.m: Stomach acid unfolds proteins for digestion.

108285.q: What can make the stomach produce gastric juice even before you eat?
a: The smell or sight of food
108285.e: Just smelling, seeing or thinking about food stimulates gastric juice through the nerves. The stomach gets ready for the meal in this way.
108285.m: Even the smell of food gets the stomach going.

a: Wave-like muscle movements in the digestive tract
108286.e: In peristalsis, the muscles of the digestive tract contract in waves. This pushes the contents along bit by bit.
108286.m: Peristalsis pushes food through the body in waves.

108287.q: Why can you swallow even when doing a handstand?
a: The stomach sucks the food in
The tongue pushes it all the way to the stomach
108287.e: The muscles of the oesophagus contract in waves. This movement works even against gravity.
108287.m: Thanks to muscle waves, swallowing works even upside down.

108288.q: Which two muscle layers work together in peristalsis?
108288.e: Circular muscles squeeze the gut, longitudinal muscles shorten it. Together they create a continuous wave.
108288.m: Circular and longitudinal muscles create peristalsis.

108289.q: What is the gut's own network of nerves sometimes called?
108289.e: There are many millions of nerve cells in the gut wall. They control the gut's movements on their own and are therefore also called the belly brain or second brain.
108289.m: The gut has its own nervous system.

108290.q: Where do the rumbling and gurgling noises in your tummy come from?
a: Gut movements push gas and liquid along
The ribs rub against each other
The heart beats against the stomach
108290.e: The muscles of the stomach and gut move gas and liquid along. This creates noises, especially when the stomach is nearly empty.
108290.m: Tummy rumbling comes from the movement of the stomach and gut.

108291.q: What is a dangerous condition called in which the contents of the gut can no longer move on?
108291.e: In a bowel obstruction, the gut is blocked or paralysed. It is an emergency that must be treated quickly in hospital.
108291.m: A bowel obstruction is a medical emergency.

108292.q: What happens to the stomach contents when you are sick?
a: They flow into the large intestine
108292.e: When you vomit, the stomach muscles and the diaphragm contract strongly. The stomach contents are pushed upwards, against the normal direction.
108292.m: When you vomit, transport runs in the wrong direction.

108293.q: Roughly how long does a mouthful take to travel down the oesophagus to the stomach?
108293.e: The oesophagus is about 25 centimetres long. The muscle wave carries a mouthful into the stomach in a few seconds.
108293.m: A mouthful reaches the stomach after a few seconds.

108294.q: Which type of muscle moves the gut without us deciding to?
108294.e: The gut wall is made of smooth muscle. It works by itself, without us controlling it consciously.
108294.m: Smooth muscles move the gut without our help.

108295.q: Which energy conversion takes place in a solar collector for hot water on the roof?
108295.e: A solar collector absorbs sunlight with a dark surface. The heat produced warms a liquid, which heats the water in the tank.
108295.m: A solar collector turns sunlight into heat.

108296.q: Which device turns kinetic energy into electrical energy?
108296.e: In a generator, a coil turns in a magnetic field. This turns kinetic energy into electrical energy.
108296.m: A generator produces electrical energy from movement.

108297.q: Which energy conversion happens in a battery while a torch is shining?
108297.e: Chemical reactions take place in the battery. Stored chemical energy is given off as electrical energy.
108297.m: A battery supplies electrical energy from chemical energy.

108298.q: Which form of energy do plants take in during photosynthesis?
108298.e: Plants use sunlight to make sugar from water and carbon dioxide. The light energy is stored as chemical energy.
108298.m: Plants store light energy as chemical energy.

108299.q: Into which form of energy does a kettle mainly turn electrical energy?
108299.e: Current flows through the kettle’s heating element and makes it very hot. This heat passes into the water.
108299.m: A kettle turns electrical energy into heat.

108300.q: Which energy conversion happens in the water wheel of an old mill?
a: Potential energy of the water into turning motion
108300.e: The water falls or flows onto the paddles of the wheel and drives it. Its potential and kinetic energy becomes the turning motion that drives the millstone.
108300.m: A water wheel uses the energy of flowing water.

108301.q: Where do our muscles get the energy for movement?
a: From the chemical energy in food
108301.e: The nutrients in food contain chemical energy. The muscle cells turn it into kinetic energy and heat.
108301.m: Muscles use the chemical energy in food.

108302.q: Which energy conversion happens when an arrow flies off in archery?
108302.e: When the bow is drawn, energy is stored in it. When released, it passes to the arrow and makes it fly fast.
108302.m: A drawn bow passes its energy to the arrow.

108303.q: Which energy conversion does an electric car use when braking to charge its battery?
108303.e: When braking, the electric motor works as a generator. In this way, some of the kinetic energy is recovered and stored in the battery.
108303.m: Electric cars can recover energy when braking.

108304.q: A bicycle light with a dynamo is shining. Where does the energy for the light come from?
a: From the movement of the legs when pedalling
From the air in the tyre
108304.e: Energy never comes from nothing. The muscles drive the wheel, the dynamo turns kinetic energy into electrical energy, and the lamp turns this into light.
108304.m: Energy is only converted, never created from nothing.

108305.q: Why does a dropped ball never bounce higher than the height it fell from?
a: It never has more energy than at the start
The Earth pulls it more strongly
The ground is always too soft
108305.e: To reach a greater height, the ball would need more potential energy than it had at the start. Without extra energy, that is impossible.
108305.m: Without extra energy, a ball never gets back to its starting height.

108306.q: A ball has 10 J of potential energy at a height of 2 m. How great is its kinetic energy just before it hits the ground, ignoring air resistance?
108306.e: Without air resistance, no energy is lost. All 10 J of potential energy is turned into kinetic energy.
108306.m: Without losses, all the potential energy becomes kinetic energy.

108307.q: A 5 kg rucksack is lifted onto a 3 m high shelf (g equals 10 N/kg). How much potential energy does it gain?
108307.e: Potential energy is calculated as m times g times h. 5 kg times 10 N/kg times 3 m gives 150 J.
108307.m: Potential energy is the product of mass, gravitational field strength and height.

108308.q: What happens to the total energy in a closed system over time?
a: At some point it becomes zero
108308.e: In a closed system, no energy is added and none is lost. That is why the sum of all forms of energy stays constant.
108308.m: In a closed system, the total energy stays constant.

108309.q: Why does a children’s swing come to a stop over time if nobody pushes it?
a: Friction turns its energy into heat
The Earth pulls it more and more strongly
108309.e: Friction in the fittings and with the air turns kinetic energy into heat. The energy is not gone, but it is no longer there as movement.
108309.m: Friction turns kinetic energy into heat.

108310.q: A skateboarder starts without any push 2 m above the bottom of a half-pipe. How high does he get on the other side if there is no friction?
108310.e: Without friction, all the energy is kept. The kinetic energy at the bottom is exactly enough to reach the starting height again.
108310.m: Without friction, you reach exactly the starting height again.

108311.q: Which English physicist showed with a stirring experiment that mechanical work is turned into heat?
108311.e: Joule used falling weights to drive a stirrer in water, and the water warmed up measurably. The unit of energy is named after him.
108311.m: Joule proved that work and heat are connected.

108312.q: What is an energy flow diagram with arrows of different widths called?
108312.e: In a Sankey diagram, a wide arrow splits into several narrower arrows. This shows where the energy flows.
108312.m: A Sankey diagram shows energy flows with arrows.

108313.q: What does the width of the arrows in an energy flow diagram show?
108313.e: The wider an arrow, the more energy flows in that direction. This lets you see the biggest shares at a glance.
108313.m: Wide arrows mean a lot of energy.

108314.q: A device receives 500 J and gives out 350 J as useful energy. How much energy does the arrow for the losses show?
108314.e: All the energy supplied is divided between useful energy and losses. 500 J minus 350 J gives 150 J.
108314.m: Energy supplied minus useful energy gives the losses.

108315.q: What must always be true in an energy flow diagram?
a: The outgoing arrows together are as wide as the incoming one
The outgoing arrows together are wider than the incoming one
There is only a single arrow
108315.e: Because energy is conserved, the sum of all outgoing energies must equal the energy supplied. Nothing is lost and nothing is added.
108315.m: In an energy flow diagram, no energy is lost.

108316.q: An LED lamp and a filament bulb give the same amount of light. Which has the narrower arrow for heat in the energy flow diagram?
108316.e: An LED lamp turns much more energy into light than a filament bulb. That is why its arrow for waste heat is much narrower.
108316.m: LED lamps give off little waste heat.

108317.q: Which outgoing arrow is the widest in the energy flow diagram of a filament bulb?
108317.e: A filament bulb gets very hot and gives off most of its energy as heat. Only a small part becomes visible light.
108317.m: For a filament bulb, the heat arrow is the widest.

108318.q: An electric motor receives 2000 J. It gives off 200 J as heat and 100 J as sound. How great is the useful energy?
108318.e: The useful energy is the energy supplied minus all losses. 2000 J minus 200 J minus 100 J gives 1700 J.
108318.m: Subtract all losses from the energy supplied.

108319.q: In an energy flow diagram, what is the energy called that serves the desired purpose?
108319.e: Useful energy is the part you actually use a device for, such as light from a lamp. The rest is shown as losses.
108319.m: Useful energy is the share you can really use.

a: Useful energy divided by energy supplied
Energy supplied divided by useful energy
108320.e: Efficiency tells you what share of the energy supplied is used. So you divide the useful energy by the energy supplied.
108320.m: Efficiency is the share of the energy supplied that is used.

108321.q: A solar system receives 4000 J of solar energy and supplies 800 J of electrical energy. What is its efficiency?
108321.e: 800 J divided by 4000 J gives 0.2. That is 20 per cent.
108321.m: An efficiency of 20 per cent means that one fifth is used.

108322.q: Why is the efficiency of a real machine always less than 100 %?
a: Electricity is too weak for it
108322.e: Friction and other processes always produce some heat that cannot be used. That is why never all of the energy arrives as useful energy.
108322.m: No real machine reaches an efficiency of 100 per cent.

108323.q: A motor has an efficiency of 30 %. What does this mean?
a: 30 % of the energy supplied is used
The motor only runs 30 % of the time
The motor only loses 30 % of the energy
108323.e: Efficiency gives the share that is used. At 30 %, 30 out of 100 parts of energy are used, and the rest mainly becomes waste heat.
108323.m: Efficiency shows how much energy is used.

108324.q: Which lamp has the highest efficiency?
108324.e: LED lamps turn a much larger share of electrical energy into light than filament bulbs. That is why they need less electricity for the same amount of light.

108325.q: Roughly what is the efficiency of an ordinary filament bulb?
108325.e: Only about 5 per cent of the electrical energy becomes visible light. That is why filament bulbs were gradually replaced by more economical lamps in many countries.
108325.m: A filament bulb turns only a small part of the electricity into light.

108326.q: A kettle has an efficiency of 90 % and receives 200 kJ. How much energy heats the water?
108326.e: You calculate 200 kJ times 0.9. That gives 180 kJ of useful energy.
108326.m: Useful energy is energy supplied times efficiency.

108327.q: Which drive typically has the highest efficiency?
108327.e: Good electric motors often reach over 90 per cent. Combustion engines usually turn less than half of the energy into movement.
108327.m: Electric motors make especially good use of energy.

108328.q: A device supplies 300 J of useful energy with an efficiency of 60 %. How much energy was supplied?
108328.e: You calculate 300 J divided by 0.6. That gives 500 J of energy supplied.
108328.m: Energy supplied is useful energy divided by efficiency.

108329.q: What is a perpetual motion machine?
a: A machine that runs for ever without any energy supply
A power station with solar cells
108329.e: A perpetual motion machine is supposed to move for ever without any energy supply and even do work. Many people have tried, but none has ever been built.
108329.m: A perpetual motion machine is a machine that cannot exist.

108330.q: Which basic principle of physics does a perpetual motion machine break?
a: The law of conservation of energy
108330.e: A perpetual motion machine would give out more energy than it takes in. According to this principle, that is impossible.
108330.m: No device gives out more energy than it receives.

108331.q: What does “perpetuum mobile” mean when translated from Latin?
a: That which moves all the time
108331.e: “Perpetuus” means continuous and “mobilis” means movable. So it means something that keeps moving all the time.
108331.m: Perpetuum mobile means that which moves all the time.

108332.q: Why has nobody ever built a working perpetual motion machine?
a: Because energy cannot come from nothing
Because the parts are too expensive
Because it is banned by law
108332.e: Every machine loses energy through friction. Without an energy supply, it therefore cannot run for ever, let alone do work.
108332.m: A perpetual motion machine is impossible.

108333.q: How do patent offices usually deal with supposed perpetual motion inventions today?
a: They grant a patent at once
108333.e: Because a perpetual motion machine is physically impossible, it does not count as an invention that can be carried out. Some offices also demand a working model.
108333.m: There is no patent for a perpetual motion machine.

108334.q: Why does even a wheel with very good bearings stop at some point?
a: Friction turns its energy into heat
The wheel gets heavier over time
108334.e: There is always some friction in bearings and with the air. This gradually turns the kinetic energy into heat.
108334.m: Friction slows down every movement at some point.

108335.q: An inventor claims his device gives out 120 J, even though it only takes in 100 J. What is true?
a: That is a very good motor
That is normal for electric motors
108335.e: The device would have an efficiency of 120 per cent. No device can give out more energy than is supplied to it.
108335.m: An efficiency above 100 per cent is impossible.

108336.q: Which classic perpetual motion design was supposed to keep turning thanks to weights on the spokes?
108336.e: In these wheels, weights on one side are supposed to hang further out and keep the wheel turning. In reality, the forces balance out, and the wheel stops.
108336.m: Even wheels with clever weights do not turn for ever.

108337.q: In which form does a pumped-storage power station store energy?
a: As potential energy of the water
108337.e: The water pumped up is higher than before and therefore has more potential energy. This is used again when it flows back down.
108337.m: Water pumped uphill stores potential energy.

108338.q: What are pumped-storage power stations especially important for in the electricity grid?
a: They supply drinking water to cities
108338.e: Electricity in the grid must always be in balance. Pumped-storage power stations can take in or give out electricity very quickly and so even out fluctuations.
108338.m: Pumped-storage power stations help to keep the grid stable.

108339.q: Why are most of Switzerland’s pumped-storage power stations in the Alps?
a: There are large differences in height between lakes there
108339.e: A pumped-storage power station needs an upper and a lower reservoir. The greater the difference in height, the more energy can be stored, and that is found in the mountains.
108339.m: Pumped-storage power stations need large differences in height.

108340.q: Roughly what is the overall efficiency of a modern pumped-storage power station?
108340.e: There are losses when pumping and when generating electricity. Altogether, about three quarters to four fifths of the energy comes back as electricity.
108340.m: A pumped-storage power station gives back about three quarters of the energy.

108341.q: What is the machine called that can both pump and generate electricity in many pumped-storage power stations?
108341.e: A pump turbine works as a pump when turning one way and as a turbine when turning the other way. This saves a second machine.
108341.m: A pump turbine can pump and generate electricity.

108342.q: What does a pumped-storage power station definitely need?
108342.e: The water must be able to flow back and forth between an upper and a lower reservoir. The greater the difference in height, the more energy can be stored.
108342.m: A pumped-storage power station needs an upper and a lower reservoir.

108343.q: 1000 kg of water is pumped up 100 m (g equals 10 N/kg). How much potential energy is stored?
108343.e: You calculate m times g times h. 1000 kg times 10 N/kg times 100 m gives 1,000,000 J, which is one megajoule.
108343.m: The higher it goes and the more water there is, the more energy is stored.

108344.q: Why is the first hill of a roller coaster usually the highest?
a: No more energy is added after it
Because the train gets heavier at the top
Because there is more air at the top
Because the train is fastest there
108344.e: After the first hill, the train runs only on its stored energy. Some of this is lost as heat through friction, so later hills have to be lower.
108344.m: Later hills of a roller coaster are lower than the first.

108345.q: Where does an unpowered roller coaster go fastest?
108345.e: At the lowest point, the most potential energy has been turned into kinetic energy. That is why the train is fastest there.
108345.m: At the bottom, the roller coaster is fastest.

108346.q: How does the train of a classic roller coaster get up the first hill?
108346.e: A motor-driven chain lift slowly pulls the train up. In this way, it gains the potential energy for the whole ride.
108346.m: The chain lift gives the roller coaster its energy.

108347.q: A roller coaster drops 45 m. Without friction, v equals √(2 · g · h) with g equal to 10 m/s². How fast is it at the bottom?
108347.e: You calculate 2 times 10 times 45, which gives 900. The square root of 900 is 30 m/s, which is 108 km/h.
108347.m: The speed can be calculated from the height of the drop.

108348.q: Which energy conversion happens when a roller coaster goes down a hill?
108348.e: Going down, the train loses height. The potential energy released makes it faster.
108348.m: Downhill, potential energy becomes kinetic energy.

108349.q: Which brakes do many modern roller coasters use without touching the rails?
108349.e: With eddy current brakes, metal plates move past strong magnets. This produces currents that slow the train down without contact and produce heat.
108349.m: Many roller coasters brake with magnets.

108350.q: What is a roller coaster called whose train is strongly accelerated by motors at the start instead of going up a lift?
108350.e: On a launched roller coaster, the train gets its energy right at the start as kinetic energy, for example from linear motors. This energy is then enough for the rest of the ride.
108350.m: A launched roller coaster is strongly accelerated at the start.

108351.q: Without friction, does the mass of the passengers affect the speed at the bottom?
a: Yes, heavy trains are much faster
Yes, light trains are much faster
Yes, but only in the rain
108351.e: Both potential energy and kinetic energy depend on mass in the same way. When you set them equal, the mass cancels out.
108351.m: Without friction, light and heavy trains go equally fast.

108352.q: Where does a swinging pendulum have the most kinetic energy?
108352.e: At the lowest point, the pendulum is fastest. There, the potential energy is smallest and the kinetic energy is greatest.
108352.m: A pendulum is fastest at the bottom.

108353.q: What is the speed of a pendulum at the turning points?
a: Half as great as at the bottom
Twice as great as at the bottom
108353.e: At the turning points, the pendulum stops briefly before swinging back. There, all the energy is stored as potential energy.
108353.m: At the turning points, a pendulum is briefly still.

108354.q: Why does the swing of a pendulum get smaller over time?
a: Air resistance and friction turn energy into heat
108354.e: With every swing, some energy is lost as heat through air resistance and friction at the pivot. Without an energy supply, the pendulum therefore comes to rest.
108354.m: Without a drive, every pendulum stops swinging at some point.

108355.q: What does the period of a pendulum mainly depend on for small swings?
108355.e: For small swings, it is mainly the length of the pendulum that decides how long one swing takes. A heavier pendulum swings just as fast.
108355.m: Long pendulums swing more slowly than short ones.

108356.q: What is the pendulum in a pendulum clock for?
108356.e: A pendulum takes almost exactly the same time for every swing. That is why it is suitable as a timekeeper that lets the clockwork move on step by step.
108356.m: The pendulum is the timekeeper of the pendulum clock.

108357.q: What did Léon Foucault show with a long pendulum in Paris in 1851?
108357.e: The plane in which the pendulum swung slowly turned relative to the floor. This shows that the Earth turns beneath the pendulum.
108357.m: Foucault’s pendulum proves that the Earth rotates.

108358.q: Which energy conversion happens when a pendulum swings up from its lowest point?
108358.e: As it swings up, the pendulum gets slower and rises higher. Kinetic energy is turned into potential energy.
108358.m: When swinging upwards, kinetic energy becomes potential energy.

108359.q: How do you keep a swing that moves like a pendulum going?
a: Add energy at the right moments
108359.e: By moving your legs and upper body at the right moment, you add energy. This makes up for the losses or even lets you swing higher.
108359.m: If you build up momentum at the right moments, you swing higher and higher.

108360.q: Roughly how long does one full swing (there and back) of a pendulum about 1 m long take?
108360.e: The pendulum formula gives a period of about 2 seconds for a length of 1 m. So one direction takes about one second.
108360.m: A pendulum 1 m long takes about one second for one direction.

108361.q: Into which forms of energy does potential energy turn when a yo-yo unrolls?
108361.e: The yo-yo falls downwards and spins faster and faster. The potential energy is then in the falling movement and in the spinning.
108361.m: A falling yo-yo moves and spins at the same time.

108362.q: Why does a yo-yo climb back up after unrolling?
a: The spinning winds the string back up
108362.e: At the bottom, the yo-yo keeps spinning and winds the string back up. In doing so, the rotational energy is turned back into potential energy.
108362.m: The spinning brings the yo-yo back up.

108363.q: Around which part in the middle of the yo-yo is the string wound?
108363.e: The two discs of a yo-yo are joined in the middle by an axle. The string is wound around it, often over a ball bearing in modern yo-yos.
108363.m: The string of a yo-yo is wound around the axle.

108364.q: What is the trick called in which the yo-yo spins in place at the bottom for a long time?
108364.e: In a sleeper, the yo-yo “sleeps” at the bottom of the string and keeps spinning. A quick tug brings it back up.
108364.m: In a sleeper, the yo-yo spins in place at the bottom.

108365.q: How does a yo-yo fall compared with a stone in free fall?
108365.e: With a yo-yo, a large part of the energy goes into spinning. Less is left for the falling movement, so it falls more slowly.
108365.m: A yo-yo falls more slowly because it spins.

108366.q: In which ancient culture are there already pictures of yo-yo-like toys on vases?
108366.e: A Greek vase from the 5th century BC shows a boy with such a toy. This makes the yo-yo one of the oldest toys.
108366.m: The yo-yo is a very old toy.

108367.q: What happens if you throw a yo-yo down hard instead of just letting it drop?
a: It spins faster at the bottom
It spins more slowly at the bottom
It does not spin at all
108367.e: The throw gives the yo-yo extra kinetic energy. At the bottom, this is in a faster spin.
108367.m: A hard throw gives the yo-yo more energy.

108368.q: What do a yo-yo and a pendulum have in common?
a: Potential and kinetic energy take turns
108368.e: In both, potential energy is turned into kinetic energy and back again. Without help, friction makes the movements smaller and smaller.
108368.m: A yo-yo and a pendulum turn energy back and forth.

108369.q: Which form of energy does the cord store in a bungee jump when it is stretched?
108369.e: The elastic cord is stretched like a spring. In the process, it takes in energy and stores it as elastic energy.
108369.m: A stretched bungee cord stores elastic energy.

108370.q: What is the jumper’s speed at the lowest point of the jump?
a: Half as great as in free fall
Twice as great as at the top
108370.e: At the lowest point, the movement reverses and the jumper is briefly still. There, most of the energy is in the stretched cord.
108370.m: At the lowest point, the jumper is still for a moment.

108371.q: Where does the idea of bungee jumping come from?
108371.e: On the island of Pentecost in Vanuatu, men have long jumped from tall wooden towers with vines tied to their feet. This land diving is seen as the model.
108371.m: Bungee jumping is modelled on land diving on Vanuatu.

108372.q: Which dam in Ticino became famous through a bungee jump in a James Bond film?
108372.e: In the 1995 film “GoldenEye”, James Bond jumps from the dam in the Verzasca valley. Today, many people jump there themselves.
108372.m: The Verzasca Dam is a famous place for bungee jumps.

108373.q: Roughly how high is the Verzasca Dam?
108373.e: The dam of Lago di Vogorno is about 220 metres high. This makes the jump one of the highest bungee jumps from a fixed structure.
108373.m: The Verzasca Dam is about 220 metres high.

108374.q: Where is a bungee jumper fastest?
a: A little below the point where the cord starts to stretch
108374.e: Even when the cord has started to stretch a little, gravity still pulls harder than the cord. So the jumper keeps getting faster until the cord pulls just as hard. Only then does it slow him down.
108374.m: The jumper is fastest when the pull of the cord equals his weight.

108375.q: Why does a bungee jumper bounce back up less and less?
a: The Earth pulls harder and harder
108375.e: The cord warms up as it stretches, and the air slows the jumper down. So with every up and down, energy is lost as heat.
108375.m: With every up and down, energy is lost as heat.

108376.q: What is the elastic cord for in bungee jumping?
a: It pulls the jumper straight back up
108376.e: The rubber cord stretches and gradually slows the jumper down. A rigid rope would stop him with a jerk and injure him.
108376.m: The elastic cord slows the jump gently.

108377.q: Why do your hands get warm when you rub them together?
a: Friction turns kinetic energy into heat
108377.e: When you rub, friction turns kinetic energy into heat. You feel this heat on your skin.

108378.q: Is energy lost when you brake on a bike?
a: No, it becomes heat that can hardly be used
Yes, it goes into the bike light
No, it is stored in the tyre
108378.e: The kinetic energy is turned into heat at the brakes and tyres. This heat spreads into the surroundings and can hardly be used any more.
108378.m: When braking, kinetic energy becomes heat.

108379.q: What is it called when energy is turned into a form that can hardly be used any more?
108379.e: The energy is still there afterwards, but usually as heat at a low temperature. It can hardly be used for work any more.
108379.m: In energy degradation, energy becomes less useful.

108380.q: Why do laptops and mobile phones get warm when they are used?
a: Some of the electrical energy becomes heat
They take in heat from your hand
108380.e: In the electronic components, current flows through resistances. In the process, some of the electrical energy always becomes heat.
108380.m: Electronic devices always give off some heat.

108381.q: What is the heat from many Swiss waste incineration plants used for?
108381.e: Burning waste produces a lot of heat. Many plants use it to generate electricity and heat homes through district heating networks.
108381.m: Heat from waste can heat houses.

108382.q: Why can the energy in lukewarm bath water hardly be used any more?
a: The difference in temperature is too small
108382.e: Heat can only be used well when there is a large difference in temperature. Lukewarm water is hardly warmer than its surroundings.
108382.m: Heat at a low temperature is of little value.

108383.q: Why do well-waxed skis make ski racers faster?
108383.e: The wax reduces the friction between the skis and the snow. This means less kinetic energy is turned into heat.
108383.m: Less friction means less energy loss.

108384.q: What is the heat called that a device gives off to its surroundings without it being used?
108384.e: Waste heat is produced as a by-product, for example by engines or computers. It is often released into the surroundings without being used.
108384.m: Waste heat is heat that escapes unused.

108385.q: At what stage does a smartphone usually use the most energy over its whole lifetime?
108385.e: A great deal of energy is needed for mining raw materials and making chips and the screen. In comparison, charging counts for much less.
108385.m: Most of a smartphone’s energy goes into making it.

108386.q: Which strawberries usually contain the most embodied energy?
a: From the farm next door in June
From the village market in summer
108386.e: Strawberries from distant countries are often transported by plane in winter. That uses a lot of energy.
108386.m: Seasonal and local fruit has less embodied energy.

108387.q: Which means of transport usually causes the most embodied energy per kilogram of goods?
108387.e: Aeroplanes need a great deal of fuel for every kilogram transported. Ships and railways are much more economical.
108387.m: Air freight uses especially large amounts of energy.

108388.q: Why does repairing a device save embodied energy?
a: No new one has to be made
108388.e: A new device brings a lot of manufacturing and transport energy with it again. If you repair, you use the energy already invested for longer.
108388.m: Repairing uses a device’s embodied energy for longer.

108389.q: Which building material needs especially large amounts of energy to make?
108389.e: To make cement, limestone is fired at very high temperatures. This needs a lot of energy, which is why concrete contains a lot of embodied energy.
108389.m: Cement and concrete contain a lot of embodied energy.

108390.q: Roughly how much energy does recycling aluminium need compared with making new aluminium?
108390.e: New aluminium is extracted from bauxite using a great deal of electricity. Melting down old aluminium needs only a small fraction of this.
108390.m: Recycling aluminium saves a great deal of energy.

108391.q: Why do you not see a product’s embodied energy on your own electricity bill?
a: It was already used before you bought it
It is only measured in the rubbish
108391.e: Embodied energy is used during manufacture and transport, that is before you own the product. That is why it does not appear on your own meter.
108391.m: Embodied energy is used before you buy a product.

108392.q: How can you recognise a tall-trunk fruit tree?
a: Very short trunk on a trellis
108392.e: In tall-trunk fruit trees, the crown only begins well above head height. Underneath, you can mow or let animals graze.
108392.m: A tall-trunk tree carries its crown high above a long trunk.

108393.q: Which small owl is typical of old tall-trunk orchards in Switzerland?
108393.e: The little owl likes to nest in holes in old fruit trees and hunts in the meadow below. As tall-trunk orchards disappeared, it became very rare in Switzerland.
108393.m: The little owl needs old fruit trees with holes.

108394.q: How is the land under the trees of a tall-trunk orchard usually used?
108394.e: Grass grows under the tall crowns and is mown or grazed by animals. This gives a double use for fruit and feed.
108394.m: In a tall-trunk orchard, a meadow grows under the trees.

108395.q: What were apples and pears from tall-trunk orchards often made into in Switzerland in the past?
108395.e: Much of the fruit from tall-trunk trees is cider fruit. It is pressed and made into sweet cider, juice or hard cider.
108395.m: Fine sweet cider is often pressed from tall-trunk fruit.

108396.q: How has the number of tall-trunk fruit trees in Switzerland developed since the 1950s?
a: It has stayed exactly the same
108396.e: Many tall-trunk trees were felled because low-trunk orchards are easier to harvest and towns and villages grew. Today only a fraction of the former trees remain.
108396.m: Tall-trunk trees have declined sharply in Switzerland.

108397.q: What is a tall-trunk orchard often called in Germany?
108397.e: The name means roughly “scattered fruit meadow”, because the trees stand loosely “scattered” across the meadow. It means the same kind of landscape.
108397.m: A Streuobstwiese is an orchard with scattered tall-trunk trees.

108398.q: Which of these apple varieties comes from Switzerland?
108398.e: Berner Rose is an old Swiss variety from the canton of Bern. Granny Smith and Pink Lady come from Australia, and Golden Delicious from the USA.
108398.m: Berner Rose is an old apple variety from Switzerland.

108399.q: Why are tall-trunk orchards important for the variety of fruit types?
a: Many old fruit varieties grow in them
Only a single variety grows there
108399.e: Old orchards often have hundreds of varieties that are missing from the shops. They are a living heritage with qualities such as resistance to disease.
108399.m: Old orchards preserve many rare fruit varieties.

108400.q: What makes old tall-trunk fruit trees particularly valuable for birds and insects?
108400.e: With age, holes, dead branches and cracks in the bark form. Hole-nesting birds, bats and many insects find shelter in them.
108400.m: The older a fruit tree is, the more animals live in it.

108401.q: What holds the stones of a dry stone wall together?
a: Only the clever way they are stacked
108401.e: A dry stone wall is built without mortar. The stones hold because of their weight and careful arrangement.
108401.m: A dry stone wall holds without any mortar.

108402.q: Which lizard even has the wall in its name?
108402.e: The common wall lizard climbs nimbly on walls and rocks. It suns itself on the warm stones and hides in the gaps.
108402.m: The common wall lizard likes to live in walls and rocks.

108403.q: Why do lizards and snakes like dry stone walls?
a: The stones store the sun's warmth
The wall is always wet and cold
The stones are made of ice
108403.e: Reptiles are cold-blooded and need warmth from outside. The sunny stones give off warmth, and the gaps offer hiding places.
108403.m: Warm stones are like a radiator for reptiles.

108404.q: Why were many dry stone walls built on steep slopes in the past?
a: To make terraces for vines and fields
108404.e: Dry stone walls hold up the earth and create flat terraces. That way vines, vegetables or cereals could be grown even on steep slopes.
108404.m: Dry stone walls make steep slopes farmable.

108405.q: Which UNESCO list was the art of dry stone walling added to in 2018, with Switzerland taking part?
108405.e: In 2018, UNESCO added the knowledge of building dry stone walls to its list of intangible cultural heritage. Several European countries, including Switzerland, submitted the application together.
108405.m: Dry stone walling is UNESCO intangible cultural heritage.

108406.q: Which plant with thick, water-storing leaves often grows in cracks in walls?
108406.e: Biting stonecrop stores water in its fleshy leaves. That way it survives drought in the cracks of sunny walls.
108406.m: Biting stonecrop stores water in thick leaves.

108407.q: Why does a retaining wall of dry stones on a slope often last a very long time?
a: Water can drain through the gaps
It is poured anew every year
It is hollow and empty inside
It is covered with plastic sheeting
108407.e: Because the gaps are open, no water builds up behind the wall. Without water pressure, the wall is under less strain.
108407.m: Water simply drains through the open gaps of a dry stone wall.

108408.q: How is a well-built dry stone retaining wall angled?
a: Leaning slightly back into the slope
Leaning strongly forward towards the road
Not at all, it hangs in the air
108408.e: The face of the wall leans slightly towards the slope. That way the wall braces itself against the pressure of the earth and does not tip forwards.
108408.m: A retaining wall leans slightly against the slope.

108409.q: Which insects like to build their nests in the gaps of sunny dry stone walls?
108409.e: Many species of wild bee nest in hollows and cracks. The warm, dry gaps of a wall are ideal for this.
108409.m: Wild bees like to nest in the gaps of dry stone walls.

108410.q: Where do the stones of a field stone heap come from?
a: They were picked off fields and meadows
They were fetched from the sea
They fell from the sky as meteorites
They were cast in a factory
108410.e: When ploughing, stones keep coming to the surface. Farmers picked them up and piled them at the edge of the field.
108410.m: Field stones were picked off the fields by hand.

108411.q: Which quick little predator uses heaps of stones and branches as hiding places from enemies?
108411.e: Stoats and weasels need lots of hiding places in open countryside. In stone heaps they are protected from birds of prey and foxes.
108411.m: Weasels need heaps of stones and branches as hiding places.

108412.q: Which animals like to sun themselves on stone heaps because the stones store warmth?
108412.e: Lizards are cold-blooded and need the sun's warmth to become active. Warm stones and lots of hiding places make stone heaps ideal for them.
108412.m: Lizards warm up on sunny stone heaps.

108413.q: Why should a newly built stone heap be partly sunk into the ground?
a: So that animals can spend the winter free from frost
So that it cannot be seen
108413.e: In the ground, the frost does not go as deep as at the surface. That way lizards and other animals find a frost-free winter home deep in the heap.
108413.m: A deep stone heap protects animals from frost.

108414.q: Why are mainly larger stones used for a stone heap?
a: So that lots of hollow spaces form
So that it becomes soft and comfortable
So that no light gets in
108414.e: Lots of gaps stay open between large stones. These hollow spaces serve animals as hiding places and passages.
108414.m: Large stones create lots of hollow spaces for animals.

108415.q: What is a field stone bank?
a: A long bank of field stones at the edge of a field
A door lock made of stone
108415.e: Where the stones were piled up along field boundaries, long, narrow banks formed. These banks still shape some farming landscapes today.
108415.m: A field stone bank is a long stone bank at the edge of a field.

108416.q: What should be left standing around a stone heap?
a: A metal fence with no gaps
108416.e: A strip of grasses and herbs offers cover and food. That way animals can move unseen between the heap and the surroundings.
108416.m: A strip of plants is what makes a stone heap really valuable.

108417.q: In nature conservation, what are small habitats such as stone heaps, branch piles or ponds called?
108417.e: Small structures cover small areas but are very important for many species. They offer hiding places, nesting sites and sunny spots in open countryside.
108417.m: Small structures are small but valuable habitats.

a: Farmland sown with native wild plants
108418.e: A wildflower fallow is sown on farmland with a mixture of native wild plants and left for several years. It offers many animals food and shelter.
108418.m: A wildflower fallow is a flowering strip of wild plants on farmland.

108419.q: What is not allowed on a wildflower fallow?
108419.e: A wildflower fallow is neither fertilised nor treated with pesticides. That way the wild plants and the animals are left undisturbed.
108419.m: On a wildflower fallow, there is no fertilising or spraying.

108420.q: Which ground-nesting gamebird is being helped in Switzerland, among other things, by wildflower fallows?
108420.e: The grey partridge lives on open farmland and has almost disappeared from Switzerland. Wildflower fallows offer it cover, nesting places and insects for the chicks.
108420.m: The grey partridge needs fallow land among the fields.

108421.q: Why are the plants of a wildflower fallow left standing in winter?
a: Insects spend the winter in the stems
So that the snow melts faster
So that cars can park there
108421.e: Insects and their larvae spend the winter in hollow stems. Birds also find food in the seed heads in winter.
108421.m: Standing stems are a winter home for insects.

108422.q: Which blue-flowering plant, whose root was once used as a coffee substitute, often grows in wildflower fallows?
108422.e: Chicory has light blue flowers and grows by paths and in fallow land. Chicory coffee was made from its roasted root.
108422.m: Chicory flowers sky blue by the wayside.

108423.q: What does the word “fallow” originally mean?
a: Farmland that rests for a while
108423.e: In the three-field system, part of the fields was left unplanted every year. This fallow land could recover.
108423.m: Nothing is grown on fallow land for a while.

108424.q: What do farmers in Switzerland receive for a wildflower fallow as a biodiversity promotion area?
a: Direct payments from the federal government
108424.e: Wildflower fallows are biodiversity promotion areas. The federal government pays contributions for them because the farmers give up a harvest.
108424.m: There are federal contributions for wildflower fallows.

108425.q: Which mammal of open fields finds cover and food in wildflower fallows?
108425.e: The brown hare lives on open farmland. It hides in the dense plants of the fallow and raises its young there.
108425.m: The brown hare likes to hide in fallow land.

a: At the edge of a field
In the middle of a forest
On the roof of a cowshed
108426.e: A conservation headland is a strip at the edge of a cereal or other crop field. It is farmed more gently there than in the rest of the field.
108426.m: Conservation headlands are at the edges of fields.

108427.q: Which plants are conservation headlands mainly meant to help?
108427.e: Many wild plants that grow along with cereals have become rare. On the headland they are allowed to flower again.
108427.m: Conservation headlands protect rare arable wild plants.

108428.q: What is not used on a conservation headland?
108428.e: On the headland, no herbicides, that is weedkillers, are used. Otherwise exactly the wild plants that are meant to be protected would disappear.
108428.m: On a conservation headland, no herbicides are sprayed.

108429.q: Is the cereal crop on a conservation headland harvested?
108429.e: The conservation headland stays part of the field. The cereal is harvested as in the rest of the field; only the care is gentler.
108429.m: The cereal on a headland is harvested too.

108430.q: Why is no nitrogen fertiliser used on a conservation headland?
a: So that the crop stays open and light
So that the cereal grows taller
So that the soil becomes acidic
108430.e: Without nitrogen fertiliser, the cereal grows less densely. That way the light-loving wild plants get enough light to grow.
108430.m: Without fertiliser, the field stays light enough for wild plants.

108431.q: What is the difference between a conservation headland and a wildflower fallow?
a: On the headland, a crop grows for harvest
Nothing grows at all on the headland
The wildflower fallow is harvested every year
108431.e: On a conservation headland, cereals or another crop are still grown and harvested. A wildflower fallow, on the other hand, is sown with wild plants and not harvested.
108431.m: The headland stays a field; the wildflower fallow does not.

108432.q: Which farmland bird benefits from open cereal crops like those on a conservation headland?
108432.e: The skylark nests on the ground in fields. In dense, tall cereal it hardly finds room, but in open crops it does.
108432.m: The skylark likes to nest in open fields.

108433.q: Why are conservation headlands good for insects?
a: The wild plants offer flowers and food
108433.e: Flowering arable wild plants provide nectar and pollen. Wild bees, butterflies and other insects live on them.
108433.m: Flowering wild plants in fields feed many insects.

a: A small group of trees and shrubs in open country
A wood store in the cellar
108434.e: A copse is a small stand of trees and shrubs in the middle of farmland. It is much smaller than a forest.
108434.m: A copse is a small island of trees in open country.

108435.q: How does a hedge differ from a copse?
a: The hedge is long and narrow
The hedge is made only of grass
108435.e: Hedges are long, narrow strips of woody plants. Copses are more compact patches.
108435.m: A hedge is a long, narrow band of woody plants.

108436.q: Which thorny shrub flowers white in spring, even before it has leaves?
108436.e: Blackthorn, also called sloe, flowers very early in the year. Its dark blue fruits become milder after the first frost.
108436.m: Blackthorn flowers white before its leaves come out.

108437.q: Which bird spikes its prey on the thorns of hedges and bushes?
108437.e: In this way, the red-backed shrike builds up a store of insects and small animals. For this it needs thorny shrubs.
108437.m: The red-backed shrike spikes its prey on thorns.

108438.q: Which shrub has bright pink fruits that look like a priest's hat and are poisonous?
108438.e: The fruits of the spindle look like the hats worn by Catholic priests. They are poisonous for people, but birds eat them.
108438.m: The spindle carries pretty but poisonous pink fruits.

108439.q: What does it mean to coppice a shrub?
a: To cut it back to just above the ground
To tie it to a wooden stick
To dig it up with its roots
To plant it in a pot
108439.e: Many shrubs sprout strongly again after being cut back hard. Hedges and copses are cared for in sections like this so that they stay dense.
108439.m: Coppiced shrubs grow back new and dense.

108440.q: Which shrub with white flower clusters carries black berries in late summer that should only be eaten cooked?
108440.e: Elder often grows in copses and at the edges of woods. Its raw berries can make you feel sick; cooked, they are made into syrup or purée.

108441.q: How do copses and hedges protect the fields near them?
a: They raise the air temperature to 40 degrees
108441.e: Woody plants slow down the wind over the fields. As a result, the soil dries out less and is blown away less.
108441.m: Hedges and copses protect fields from wind.

108442.q: Which shrub in copses provides nuts that squirrels and dormice eat?
108442.e: Hazel forms hazelnuts in autumn. Its catkins flower as early as February and provide early pollen.
108442.m: Hazel provides nuts for many animals.

108443.q: Why is ecological networking important for animals?
a: They no longer have to look for food
108443.e: Many animals have to travel to find food, to breed or to find new territories. Connected habitats make this possible.
108443.m: Linked habitats let animals move around.

108444.q: What are small habitats called that make it easier for animals to cross open land, like stones in a stream?
108444.e: Stepping-stone habitats lie at certain distances across the landscape. Animals can move from one to the next and rest in between.
108444.m: Stepping stones help animals to cross open land.

108445.q: How can wild animals safely cross a motorway?
a: Only at night in traffic jams
108445.e: Wildlife bridges are covered with soil, grass and bushes. Deer, foxes and other animals can cross the motorway on them.
108445.m: Wildlife bridges link habitats across roads.

108446.q: What can farmers in Switzerland receive if they take part in a regional networking project?
a: Extra contributions from the federal government
A ban on building on their house
108446.e: There are networking contributions for biodiversity promotion areas laid out according to a regional networking project. That way the areas are spread out in a sensible way.
108446.m: Linked biodiversity areas are especially rewarded.

108447.q: What is meant by habitat fragmentation?
108447.e: Roads, railway lines and built-up areas split habitats into small pieces. Many animals can hardly get past these barriers.
108447.m: Roads cut up the habitats of many animals.

108448.q: What threatens a small group of animals living in an isolated habitat?
108448.e: Without contact with other groups, close relatives mate with each other and genetic diversity decreases. Even small disturbances can wipe out the group.
108448.m: Isolated small populations die out more easily.

108449.q: Which night-active animals like to fly along hedges and rows of trees as if following a guideline?
108449.e: Many bats use ultrasound to find their way along lines of trees and shrubs. Without hedges, they find the way to their hunting grounds less easily.
108449.m: Bats follow hedges like a road.

108450.q: What is a network of habitats called between which animals and plants can move and mix?
108450.e: In a habitat network, habitats are linked by corridors and stepping stones. This is the aim of ecological networking.
108450.m: A habitat network links individual habitats.

108451.q: What is meant by arable weed flora?
a: Wild plants growing among crop plants
Plants that grow only in greenhouses
Trees at the edge of a forest
108451.e: Arable wild plants grow together with cereals and other crops. They used to be called, often disapprovingly, weeds.
108451.m: Arable wild plants grow wild among the crop plants.

108452.q: Which field plant with bright red flowers often grows at the edge of cereal fields?
108452.e: The common poppy has large, red, thin petals. It sprouts on open, dug-over soil.
108452.m: The common poppy turns field edges bright red.

108453.q: Which field plant flowers a strong blue among the cereals?
108453.e: The cornflower is typical of cereal fields. It used to be so common that it became a symbol of the cornfield.
108453.m: The cornflower flowers blue in the cereal field.

108454.q: Which yellow-flowering field plant belongs to the cabbage family (crucifers)?
108454.e: Charlock has four yellow petals arranged like a cross. It often grows in cereal and oilseed rape fields.
108454.m: Charlock flowers yellow and is a crucifer.

108455.q: Why have many arable wild plants become rare today?
a: Because of weedkillers and heavy fertilising
Because birds eat all the seeds
108455.e: Herbicides kill the wild plants, and heavily fertilised cereals grow so densely that they no longer get any light.
108455.m: Sprays and fertiliser have crowded out many arable wild plants.

108456.q: Which field plant with white flowers and a yellow centre is traditionally used as a tea?
108456.e: Chamomile grows in fields and by paths. The base of its flower head is hollow inside, which tells it apart from similar species.
108456.m: Chamomile is a well-known tea plant from the fields.

108457.q: Why do vanished arable wild plants sometimes reappear after many years?
a: Their seeds survive for a long time in the soil
They fall from the sky with the rain
108457.e: Many seeds can still sprout after years in the soil. This seed bank sprouts when conditions are right again.
108457.m: A seed bank of old field plants lies sleeping in the soil.

108458.q: Which rare arable wild plant has blue flowers with a long spur?
108458.e: Forking larkspur has flowers with a long spur. It is a typical, now rare, arable wild plant on lime-rich soils.
108458.m: Forking larkspur is a rare arable wild plant with a spur.

108459.q: What colour are the flowers of the corncockle?
108459.e: The corncockle has large, purplish red flowers. In the past it stood out clearly in cereal fields.
108459.m: The corncockle flowers purplish red among the cereals.

108460.q: What are plants such as the corncockle called, which grow as wild companions in cereal fields?
108460.e: Corncockle, cornflower and common poppy grow among the cereals. Many of these arable companion plants have become rare today.
108460.m: The corncockle is an arable companion plant.

108461.q: Why did farmers fear the corncockle in the past?
a: Its poisonous seeds got into the flour
108461.e: Corncockle seeds contain poisonous saponins. If they were ground with the cereal, the bread could cause poisoning.
108461.m: Corncockle seeds in flour made bread poisonous.

108462.q: What almost made the corncockle disappear from Central Europe?
108462.e: Corncockle seeds used to be sown again together with the cereal. Since seed grain has been cleaned thoroughly, it has lost this route.
108462.m: Clean seed grain almost drove out the corncockle.

108463.q: Where did the corncockle typically grow in the past?
108463.e: The corncockle was a typical companion of rye and wheat. Its name refers to “corn”, that is, cereal.
108463.m: The corncockle is an old companion of cereals.

108464.q: How long does a corncockle plant live?
108464.e: The corncockle sprouts, flowers and forms seeds within one year. Then the plant dies and only the seeds survive.
108464.m: The corncockle is an annual plant.

108465.q: Which blue field flower often grows together with the corncockle in wildflower mixtures?
108465.e: Cornflower and corncockle used to be typical flowers among cereals. Today they are sown together in flower meadows and gardens.
108465.m: Cornflower and corncockle are old companions of cereals.

108466.q: Where do you often come across the corncockle again today?
108466.e: In the wild, the corncockle has become very rare. But it is sown again in flower meadow mixtures, gardens and conservation projects.
108466.m: Today the corncockle often lives on in wildflower sowings.

108467.q: What is a branch pile made of?
108467.e: Caring for hedges and trees produces a lot of cuttings. Stacked up, they form a valuable habitat.
108467.m: A branch pile is stacked up from cuttings.

108468.q: Which prickly mammal likes to spend the winter in a branch pile?
108468.e: The hedgehog hibernates in a sheltered nest. A branch pile with leaves is ideal for this.
108468.m: The hedgehog likes to sleep through winter in a branch pile.

108469.q: Why should you not simply set fire to a branch pile?
a: Animals such as hedgehogs may be sleeping in it
It only burns in the rain
It is too wet for a fire
The branches would grow back at once
108469.e: Hedgehogs, toads and many insects hide in branch piles. If you have to burn one, you should move it to a new spot first.
108469.m: Before burning a branch pile, you must check it for animals.

108470.q: Which small brown bird with an upturned tail likes to build its nest in dense branches?
108470.e: The wren is one of the smallest birds in Switzerland. It builds round nests in dense undergrowth and branch piles.
108470.m: The tiny wren nests in dense undergrowth.

108471.q: Which legless lizard likes to hide under branch piles?
108471.e: The slow worm looks like a snake but is a lizard. It hunts slugs and worms in damp ground.
108471.m: The slow worm is a lizard without legs.

108472.q: What breaks down the wood of a branch pile over the years?
108472.e: Fungi, beetle larvae and other small creatures slowly break down the wood. This produces valuable humus.
108472.m: Fungi and insects turn dead wood into soil.

108473.q: What can grow over time from a loosely stacked bank of branches?
108473.e: Birds sit on the bank of branches and drop seeds. Shrubs grow from them, and so a living hedge forms, called a Benjes hedge.
108473.m: A hedge can grow from a bank of branches.

108474.q: Why is a wooden nesting chamber often built into branch piles for weasels?
a: As a protected place for the young
As a winter home for bats
As a feeding place for birds
108474.e: Weasels need dry, protected chambers to raise their young. A nest box in a branch or stone heap offers exactly that.
108474.m: A chamber in a branch pile serves weasels as a nursery.

a: A willow whose branches are cut back regularly
A pasture for cows on the alp
108475.e: With a pollarded willow, all the branches are cut off at the same height every few years. Over time, a thick “head” forms there.
108475.m: A pollarded willow is made by regular cutting back.

108476.q: What were the shoots of pollarded willows mainly used for in the past?
108476.e: The long, bendy shoots are good for weaving. Baskets, fences and mats were made from them.
108476.m: Baskets are woven from willow shoots.

108477.q: What often forms in the trunk of old pollarded willows over time?
108477.e: The trunk of old pollarded willows often becomes hollow and rotten. Birds, bats and insects live in these hollows.
108477.m: Old pollarded willows often have hollow trunks.

108478.q: Why are old pollarded willows so valuable for insects?
a: Many beetle larvae live in the rotting wood
Their leaves are made of sugar
108478.e: The old, partly rotten wood offers food and a home. The larvae of rare longhorn beetles, for example, develop in it.
108478.m: Old pollarded willows are a home for many insects.

108479.q: Where do pollarded willows typically grow?
a: By streams and in damp places
108479.e: Willows love damp soil. That is why pollarded willows often stand in rows along streams and ditches.
108479.m: Pollarded willows like to stand by water.

108480.q: What happens if a pollarded willow is no longer cut?
a: The heavy crown can split the trunk
It turns into a fir tree
108480.e: The branches get thicker and heavier. Over time, the head can break apart and the tree can die.

108481.q: How can willows be propagated particularly easily?
a: A fresh branch is pushed into the ground
108481.e: Willow branches quickly form roots when pushed into damp soil. New pollarded willows are planted like this too.
108481.m: A willow branch in the ground quickly takes root.

108482.q: Which well-known painkiller is modelled on a substance from willow bark?
108482.e: Even long ago, people chewed willow bark against pain. From its active substance, chemists developed acetylsalicylic acid, which became known as aspirin.
108482.m: The model for aspirin comes from willow bark.

108483.q: Why are willow catkins particularly important for bees in spring?
a: They provide pollen and nectar very early
108483.e: Willows flower as early as March, when little else is in flower. Bees and bumblebees find their first food there.
108483.m: Willow catkins are early bee forage.

a: A passage for wild animals between habitats
108484.e: Wildlife corridors are connections along which animals move from one habitat to another. They often lead across obstacles such as roads.
108484.m: Wildlife corridors are routes for wild animals.

108485.q: What is a planted bridge called on which animals can cross a motorway?
108485.e: Wildlife bridges, also called green bridges, are covered with soil, grass and shrubs. Animals use them because they seem like natural ground.
108485.m: On a wildlife bridge, animals safely cross the motorway.

108486.q: How do road builders help toads and frogs to cross a road safely?
a: With loud music at the roadside
108486.e: Guide fences lead the amphibians to small tunnels under the road. That way they reach their spawning waters without being run over.
108486.m: Amphibian tunnels save toads from death on the road.

108487.q: Which large wild cat in Switzerland needs wide, connected habitats?
108487.e: The lynx lives in large territories in forests. Young lynxes have to travel far to find a territory of their own.
108487.m: The lynx needs large, connected forests.

108488.q: Why are motorways almost impossible for roe deer and red deer to cross?
a: They are fenced and very busy
108488.e: Wildlife fences do keep animals off the road, but they also block their routes. Without bridges or underpasses, the motorway remains a barrier.

108489.q: Which problem for people do wildlife corridors also help to reduce?
a: Collisions with wild animals on roads
108489.e: When animals use safe crossings, fewer of them run onto the road. This protects both animals and drivers.
108489.m: Wildlife corridors prevent collisions with wild animals.

108490.q: What are hedges and fences around a wildlife bridge for?
a: They guide the animals to the bridge
They keep animals away from the bridge
They serve as a feeding trough
108490.e: Guiding structures lead the animals straight to the crossing. Without them, many animals would never find the bridge.
108490.m: Guiding structures lead wild animals to the safe bridge.

108491.q: Apart from roads, what else can interrupt a wildlife corridor?
108491.e: When towns and villages grow together, no passage is left free. That is why corridors are meant to be kept open in land-use planning.
108491.m: Towns growing together block the way for wild animals.

108591.q: Which organ is the body's most important detox centre?
108591.e: The liver breaks down many toxins, medicines and alcohol or makes them harmless. Afterwards they can be got rid of via the kidneys or the bile.
108591.m: The liver is the body's great detox centre.

108592.q: Into which substance does the liver turn the toxic ammonia from breaking down protein?
108592.e: Breaking down protein produces toxic ammonia. The liver turns it into harmless urea, which the kidneys remove in urine.
108592.m: The liver turns toxic ammonia into harmless urea.

108593.q: To which organ does blood from the gut flow first, so that absorbed substances can be checked?
108593.e: The nutrient-rich blood from the stomach and gut flows first to the liver. It processes the substances and makes toxic ones harmless.
108593.m: Blood from the gut flows to the liver first.

108594.q: What helps alcohol in the blood to be broken down faster?
a: Nothing, the liver simply needs time
108594.e: The liver breaks down alcohol slowly and steadily. Coffee, showers or fresh air do not speed this up.
108594.m: Alcohol is broken down only slowly, and nothing can speed up the liver.

108595.q: Which liquid does the liver make, which it also uses to send waste substances into the gut?
108595.e: The liver makes bile every day. With it, waste substances get into the gut, and bile also helps to digest fat.
108595.m: Bile carries waste substances from the liver into the gut.

108596.q: Where is bile stored before it flows into the gut?
108596.e: The gall bladder lies on the underside of the liver. It stores and concentrates the bile and releases it into the duodenum after a fatty meal.
108596.m: The gall bladder stores the bile that the liver makes.

108597.q: Which liver disease often results from years of heavy drinking and scars the organ?
108597.e: In cirrhosis, healthy liver tissue is gradually replaced by scar tissue. The liver can then do its jobs, including detoxifying, less and less well.
108597.m: Too much alcohol can permanently scar the liver.

108598.q: What special ability does the liver have compared with many other organs?
108598.e: The liver regenerates well: if part of it is removed, the remaining tissue grows back. That is why a living person can even donate part of their liver.
108598.m: The liver can regrow lost tissue.

108599.q: Where in the body is the liver?
a: In the upper right of the belly
In the lower left of the belly
108599.e: The liver lies in the upper right of the belly, directly below the diaphragm. It is partly protected by the ribs.
108599.m: The liver lies in the upper right of the belly below the diaphragm.

108600.e: Glycogen is a polysaccharide, which means it is built from a great many sugar units. Humans and animals use it to store sugar as a quick energy reserve.
108600.m: Glycogen is the sugar store of humans and animals.

108601.q: In which two tissues do humans store the most glycogen?
108601.e: The liver and the skeletal muscles contain most of the glycogen. Because there is so much muscle, the muscles even store more in total than the liver.
108601.m: The liver and muscles are the big glycogen stores.

108602.q: What building blocks is glycogen made of?
108602.e: Glycogen is a long, highly branched chain of glucose molecules. When needed, single glucose units are split off again.
108602.m: Glycogen is made of many glucose units.

108603.q: Which hormone makes sure that sugar is stored as glycogen after a meal?
108603.e: After a meal, blood sugar rises and the pancreas releases insulin. Insulin helps the liver and muscles take in glucose and store it as glycogen.
108603.m: Insulin makes sugar be stored as glycogen.

108604.q: Which hormone makes the liver break down glycogen when blood sugar is too low?
108604.e: Glucagon is also made in the pancreas. It makes the liver split glycogen and release glucose into the blood.
108604.m: Glucagon takes sugar out of the liver's glycogen store.

108605.q: What does a muscle use its own glycogen for?
108605.e: Muscle glycogen mainly serves as energy for the muscle itself during movement. The liver, on the other hand, releases glucose from its glycogen into the blood and so supplies the whole body.
108605.m: Muscles use their glycogen mainly for themselves.

108606.q: Which storage substance made from glucose do plants form instead of glycogen?
108606.e: Plants store sugar as starch, for example in potatoes or cereal grains.
108606.m: Plants store sugar as starch, animals as glycogen.

108607.q: Why do endurance athletes like to eat pasta before a competition?
108607.e: Pasta contains a lot of starch, which is digested into glucose. From this the body fills up its glycogen stores in the muscles and liver, which are used up quickly in endurance sport.
108607.m: Carbohydrates fill the glycogen stores for sport.

108608.q: What is glycogen also called because it resembles the storage substance of plants?
108608.e: Glycogen is built similarly to plant starch, only more branched. That is why it is often called animal starch.
108608.m: Glycogen is also called animal starch.

108609.q: What does the word hepatitis mean?
108609.e: The Greek word “hepar” means liver, and the ending “-itis” stands for inflammation. So hepatitis is an inflammation of the liver.
108609.m: Hepatitis is an inflammation of the liver.

108610.q: What is the most common cause of hepatitis?
108610.e: Hepatitis is most often caused by hepatitis viruses. The main types are A, B, C, D and E.
108610.m: Most cases of liver inflammation are caused by viruses.

108611.q: How do people usually catch hepatitis A?
108611.e: Hepatitis A viruses leave the body in poo and can be passed on through contaminated drinking water or food. Washing your hands thoroughly protects you.
108611.m: Thorough hand washing protects against hepatitis A.

108612.q: How are the hepatitis B and C viruses mainly passed on?
108612.e: These viruses pass from person to person mainly through blood, for example through shared needles. That is why hospitals use sterile single-use needles.
108612.m: Hepatitis B and C are mainly passed on through blood.

108613.q: Against which forms of hepatitis is there a vaccine?
108613.e: There are effective vaccines against hepatitis A and hepatitis B. There is no vaccine against hepatitis C yet, but there are good medicines.
108613.m: You can be vaccinated against hepatitis A and B.

108614.q: A case of hepatitis does not heal and lasts for years. What is such a long-lasting illness called?
108614.e: An illness is called chronic if it lasts a long time or keeps coming back. An acute illness starts suddenly and is usually over after a short time. Hepatitis C often becomes chronic.
108614.m: A chronic illness lasts a very long time.

108615.q: Which sign can appear with hepatitis?
108615.e: If the liver is inflamed, it can no longer break down the yellow pigment bilirubin properly. It settles in the skin and eyes; this is called jaundice.
108615.m: With an inflamed liver, the skin and eyes can turn yellow.

108616.q: What is the best way to protect yourself against hepatitis B?
108616.e: There is an effective vaccine against hepatitis B, which is recommended for teenagers in Switzerland. It also protects against hepatitis D at the same time.
108616.m: A vaccine protects against hepatitis B.

108617.q: Which job of the liver can be disturbed by hepatitis?
a: It breaks down toxins in the body
108617.e: The liver is the most important detox organ. It breaks down alcohol and medicines, for example. If it is inflamed, it works less well.

108618.q: Which parts of the body turn yellow with jaundice?
a: The skin and the whites of the eyes
108618.e: In jaundice, a yellow pigment builds up in the tissues. It is often seen first in the whites of the eyes, then in the skin.
108618.m: With jaundice, the skin and the whites of the eyes turn yellow.

108619.q: What causes the yellow colour in jaundice?
a: A yellow waste substance in the blood
108619.e: When red blood cells are broken down, a yellow substance called bilirubin is made. If the liver cannot remove it fast enough, it settles in the skin and eyes.
108619.m: In jaundice, a yellow waste substance in the blood colours the skin.

108620.q: What is bilirubin made from in the body?
108620.e: Red blood cells live for about 120 days. When their pigment haemoglobin is broken down, bilirubin is made, which the liver processes further.
108620.m: Bilirubin comes from breaking down red blood pigment.

108621.q: Which organ is often ill when someone has jaundice?
108621.e: The liver processes the yellow waste substance from the blood. If it is ill, the substance builds up and the skin and eyes turn yellow.
108621.m: Jaundice often points to a problem with the liver.

108622.q: How is the common jaundice of newborn babies often treated?
a: With a brace on the teeth
108622.e: Newborn babies often have mild jaundice. If it is stronger, blue light helps to break down the bilirubin in the skin.
108622.m: Blue light helps against jaundice in newborn babies.

108623.q: What can block the bile duct and so cause jaundice?
108623.e: A gallstone can block the flow of bile into the gut. The bilirubin then backs up into the blood and jaundice develops.
108623.m: A blocked bile duct can cause jaundice.

108624.q: How does urine often change in jaundice caused by liver disease?
108624.e: When there is a lot of bilirubin in the blood, the kidneys get rid of some of it. The urine then turns dark, often like dark beer, while the poo can become pale.
108624.m: With jaundice, the urine can turn dark.

108625.q: Why is jaundice so common in newborn babies in their first days of life?
