109412.e: Typhoid is caused by Salmonella Typhi. The disease is widespread in countries with poor water supplies.
109412.m: Typhoid is caused by a type of salmonella.

109413.q: How long does it usually take from catching salmonella to the first symptoms?
a: A few hours to about 3 days
109413.e: The incubation period of salmonella infection is short, usually a few hours to a few days. That is why the cause is often a meal from the day before.
109413.m: Salmonella usually make you ill within hours to a few days.

109414.e: Prevention comes from the Latin “praevenire”, to come before. Addiction prevention aims to stop an addiction from developing at all.
109414.m: Prevention means stopping something before it starts.

109415.q: What is a typical feature of an addiction?
109415.e: Someone who is addicted can no longer decide for themselves how much they use or when they stop. Experts call this loss of control.
109415.m: With an addiction, you lose control over your use.

109416.q: What are the unpleasant symptoms called when an addict suddenly stops using their drug?
109416.e: The body has got used to the substance. When it is missing, withdrawal symptoms such as restlessness, shaking or sleep problems appear.
109416.m: Withdrawal symptoms show that the body is dependent.

109417.q: What is pressure from friends to join in with something called?
109417.e: Peer pressure arises when you want to belong. Anyone who can say “no” is better protected against risky use.
109417.m: Saying no protects against peer pressure.

109418.q: Which addiction is a behavioural addiction without a substance?
109418.e: In gambling addiction, no substance is taken. It is the behaviour itself, gambling for money, that causes the dependence.
109418.m: A behaviour such as gambling can also be addictive.

109419.q: Which phone number do children and teenagers in Switzerland call for advice when they are worried?
109419.e: On the number 147, Pro Juventute advises children and teenagers around the clock. 117 is the police, 118 the fire brigade and 144 the ambulance.
109419.m: The number 147 helps young people in Switzerland when they are worried.

109420.q: What best strengthens children and teenagers against the dangers of addiction?
a: As much screen time as possible
109420.e: Anyone who believes in themselves, can solve problems and feels supported by others is less likely to turn to drugs. Such protective factors are at the heart of addiction prevention.
109420.m: Self-confidence and good friendships protect against addiction.

109421.q: Which federal office in Switzerland is responsible for health and national prevention programmes?
109421.e: The Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH) runs national strategies, for example on addiction and non-communicable diseases. It works with the cantons and specialist bodies to do this.
109421.m: The FOPH looks after the health of the population in Switzerland.

109422.q: Which plant does nicotine come from?
109422.e: Nicotine is found naturally in the leaves of the tobacco plant. The plant uses it to protect itself from insects.
109422.m: Nicotine comes from the tobacco plant.

109423.q: Which substance in tobacco smoke is mainly what makes people addicted?
109423.e: Nicotine acts on the reward system in the brain and quickly makes people addicted. Tar and other substances mainly harm the lungs and blood vessels.
109423.m: Nicotine is the substance that makes smokers addicted.

109424.q: How quickly does nicotine reach the brain when someone smokes?
109424.e: Through the lungs, nicotine gets into the blood very quickly and reaches the brain within seconds. This fast effect adds greatly to the addiction.
109424.m: Nicotine reaches the brain in seconds.

109425.e: The French envoy Jean Nicot brought tobacco to the French court in the 16th century. The tobacco plant Nicotiana and nicotine bear his name.
109425.m: Nicotine is named after the Frenchman Jean Nicot.

109426.q: What else was nicotine used for in the past?
109426.e: Nicotine is a strong nerve poison. That is why it used to be used against insects; today this is banned in many countries.

109427.q: What is heated and breathed in with an e-cigarette?
109427.e: An e-cigarette vaporises a liquid that often contains nicotine. Even without burning, the vapour can contain harmful substances.
109427.m: E-cigarettes vaporise a liquid that often contains nicotine.

109428.q: Which poisonous gas in tobacco smoke hinders the transport of oxygen in the blood?
109428.e: Carbon monoxide binds much more strongly to the red blood pigment than oxygen does. As a result, the blood carries less oxygen.
109428.m: Carbon monoxide from tobacco smoke robs the blood of oxygen.

109430.e: Snus is moist tobacco in small pouches that are placed under the lip. The nicotine gets into the blood through the lining of the mouth.
109430.m: Snus is placed under the lip and contains nicotine.

109431.q: Which form of media addiction has the WHO included as an illness in ICD-11?
109431.e: The World Health Organization lists gaming addiction (“gaming disorder”) in its list of diseases, ICD-11. ICD-11 has been in force since 2022.
109431.m: Gaming addiction is recognised as an illness by the WHO.

109432.q: What is a warning sign of media addiction?
109432.e: Anyone who neglects friends, hobbies and school because of their phone or games is showing a warning sign. Loss of control and irritability without the device often come too.
109432.m: If media make you neglect everything else, take care.

109433.q: What does the abbreviation FOMO stand for?
109433.e: FOMO stands for “fear of missing out”. The fear of missing something makes many people check their phone constantly.
109433.m: FOMO is the fear of missing out.

109434.q: Which sleep hormone is held back by bright screen light in the evening?
109434.e: Blue light from screens holds back the production of melatonin. You get tired later and find it harder to fall asleep.
109434.m: Screen light in the evening disturbs sleep.

109435.q: What is it called when someone ignores the person they are with and looks at their phone?
109435.e: Phubbing is made up of “phone” and “snubbing”. The other person often feels they are not being taken seriously.
109435.m: Phubbing means ignoring others because of your phone.

109436.q: Which messenger substance in the brain plays a part when likes give us a good feeling?
109436.e: Dopamine is a messenger substance of the reward system. Rewards such as likes or winning in games can release it and make you want more.
109436.m: Dopamine creates the feeling of reward in the brain.

109437.q: What is a sensible rule against too much screen time?
a: Always keep your phone within reach
Only stop when the battery is flat
109437.e: Fixed times without a phone, for example during meals or homework, help keep media use under control.
109437.m: Fixed phone times help against too much screen time.

109438.q: Which app feature tempts you to keep swiping because the content never ends?
109438.e: With infinite scrolling, new content keeps loading. There is no natural stopping point, so you easily lose track of time.
109438.m: Infinite scrolling makes time on your phone fly by.

109439.q: What helps against too much phone time at night?
a: Charging the phone outside the bedroom
Putting the phone under your pillow
109439.e: If the phone is not next to the bed, no messages disturb your sleep. That makes it easier not to look at the screen again.
109439.m: The phone sleeps best in another room.

109440.q: Where does the foundation Addiction Switzerland work?
a: Only in the canton of Zurich
109440.e: Addiction Switzerland is based in Lausanne but works for the whole of Switzerland and in several national languages.
109440.m: Addiction Switzerland works for the whole of Switzerland.

109441.q: What kind of organisation is Addiction Switzerland?
109441.e: Addiction Switzerland is a non-profit, independent foundation. It does research, provides information and campaigns for prevention.
109441.m: Addiction Switzerland is a non-profit foundation.

109442.q: What is Addiction Switzerland called in French?
109442.e: The foundation works in several national languages. In French it is known as “Addiction Suisse”; in German it is called “Sucht Schweiz”.
109442.m: Addiction Suisse is the French name of Addiction Switzerland.

109443.q: How does Addiction Switzerland find out how many young people smoke or drink alcohol?
109443.e: Addiction Switzerland regularly surveys pupils aged 11 to 15, anonymously and voluntarily. This shows how use is changing.
109443.m: Addiction Switzerland asks young people about their behaviour.

109444.q: Why does the foundation have the general name “Addiction Switzerland”?
a: It deals with all kinds of addiction
109444.e: In the past, alcohol was the main focus. Today it covers all forms of addiction, from tobacco and cannabis to gambling and online addiction.
109444.m: Addiction Switzerland deals with all forms of addiction.

109445.q: Which tasks does Addiction Switzerland carry out?
109445.e: Addiction Switzerland develops prevention projects, researches addictive behaviour and informs professionals, parents and young people. Punishment and police work are not part of it.
109445.m: Addiction Switzerland does research, informs and works to prevent addiction.

109446.q: Which topics does Addiction Switzerland deal with?
109446.e: The foundation deals with substances such as alcohol, tobacco and cannabis. Behavioural addictions such as gambling and online addiction are also included.
109446.m: Addiction Switzerland deals with substance and behavioural addictions.

109447.q: From what age are you usually allowed to buy beer and wine in Switzerland?
109447.e: In most cantons, beer and wine may be sold from the age of 16. A higher age limit applies to spirits.
109447.m: In Switzerland, beer and wine are usually available from 16.

109448.q: From what age may spirits such as schnapps be sold in Switzerland?
109448.e: Under the Alcohol Act, spirits may not be sold to anyone under 18. This also includes alcopops.
109448.m: Schnapps and alcopops are only available from 18.

109449.q: Since October 2024, from what age may tobacco products be sold throughout Switzerland?
109449.e: Under the Tobacco Products Act, sales to minors have been banned throughout Switzerland since 1 October 2024. This also applies to e-cigarettes.
109449.m: In Switzerland, tobacco and e-cigarettes are only available from 18.

109450.q: Why may alcopops only be sold from 18 in Switzerland?
109450.e: Alcopops are sweet mixed drinks containing spirits. Because they contain distilled spirits, the age limit of 18 applies.
109450.m: Alcopops contain spirits and are for over-18s only.

109451.q: What do the PEGI labels on video games stand for?
a: The country where it was made
109451.e: PEGI is a European system for age-rating games. The levels 3, 7, 12, 16 and 18 show from what age a game is suitable.
109451.m: PEGI numbers show from what age a game is suitable.

109452.q: How do the authorities check whether shops sell alcohol to under-18s?
109452.e: In test purchases, young people try to buy alcohol on behalf of the authorities. This shows whether the staff check people's age.
109452.m: Test purchases show whether the rules protecting young people are followed.

109453.q: According to their terms of use, from what age do many social networks allow you to have your own account?
109453.e: Many platforms such as Instagram or TikTok require a minimum age of 13. However, this is often only weakly checked.
109453.m: Many social networks are only allowed from 13.

109454.q: What can parents set up on devices to protect children from unsuitable content?
109454.e: Parental controls can limit apps, content and screen time. But they do not replace talking about media.
109454.m: Parental controls protect against unsuitable content.

109455.q: What shape is a healthy spine when seen from the side?
109455.e: Seen from the side, the spine curves in a double S shape. This shape absorbs shocks when you walk and jump.
109455.m: The spine has the shape of a double S.

109456.q: What can lead to a rounded back in many children?
a: Sitting hunched for long periods and little exercise
109456.e: Anyone who often sits slumped and moves little has weak back muscles. Over time, a rounded back can then develop.
109456.m: A lot of hunched sitting can lead to a rounded back.

109457.q: Which way of sitting is best for your back?
a: Only sitting on the edge of the chair
109457.e: In active sitting, you change your position often. This loads and unloads the spinal discs in turn and keeps them well supplied with nutrients.
109457.m: The best sitting position is always the next one.

109458.q: What is a sideways curve of the spine called?
109458.e: In scoliosis, the spine is bent and twisted to the side. It often develops during growth and is therefore checked in children.
109458.m: Scoliosis is a sideways curve of the spine.

109459.q: How do you lift a heavy box without straining your back?
a: From the knees with a straight back
With a rounded back and straight legs
With a jerk using one arm
109459.e: When lifting, you bend your knees, keep your back straight and hold the load close to your body. This way the strong leg muscles do the work instead of the spine.
109459.m: Lift heavy things from the knees with a straight back.

109460.q: What best strengthens the back and prevents posture problems?
109460.e: Strong stomach and back muscles support the spine like a corset. Exercise and targeted training prevent back problems.
109460.m: Strong core muscles protect the back.

109461.q: What is it called when the lower back curves forward too much?
109461.e: In a hollow back, the lower spine curves forward too much. Weak stomach muscles make it more likely.
109461.m: A lower back that curves forward too much is called a hollow back.

109462.q: What happens if you tilt your head far forward while looking at your phone?
a: The neck muscles are put under more strain
109462.e: The further the head tips forward, the harder the neck muscles have to work to hold it. This is also called “text neck”.
109462.m: It is better to hold your phone at eye level.

109463.q: Roughly how heavy should a packed school bag be at most?
a: Around 10 per cent of body weight
Around 50 per cent of body weight
Exactly as heavy as the child
Around 1 per cent of body weight
109463.e: Experts recommend that a packed school bag should not be much more than about 10 per cent of body weight. Otherwise it puts too much strain on the back.
109463.m: A school bag should weigh about a tenth of your body weight.

109464.q: A child weighs 35 kg. How heavy may their school bag be according to the 10 per cent rule?
109464.e: 10 per cent of 35 kg is 35 × 0.1 = 3.5 kg. The packed bag should not weigh more than that.
109464.m: To work out ten per cent, divide by ten.

109465.q: How should you carry a school bag?
a: With both straps on your back
On one strap over one shoulder
109465.e: With both straps, the weight is spread evenly over both shoulders. Carrying it on one side can lead to poor posture.
109465.m: Always carry your school bag with both straps.

109466.q: Where do you pack heavy books in a school bag?
109466.e: Heavy things belong close to your back. This keeps the centre of gravity close to your body and the bag pulls back less.
109466.m: Pack heavy things close to your back.

109467.q: Why do school bags have bright colours and reflectors?
a: So children can be seen easily in traffic
109467.e: Bright colours stand out during the day, and reflectors shine in headlights. This way drivers see children on their way to school earlier.
109467.m: Bright colours and reflectors make children visible on the way to school.

109469.q: What is a chest or hip strap on a school bag for?
a: It spreads the load and holds the bag in place
109469.e: Chest and hip straps keep the bag close to the body. A hip strap also passes some of the weight onto the pelvis.
109469.m: A hip strap takes strain off the shoulders.

109470.q: An empty school bag weighs 1.2 kg. Add books weighing 2.5 kg and a mid-morning snack weighing 0.3 kg. How heavy is the bag?
109470.e: 1.2 kg + 2.5 kg + 0.3 kg = 4 kg. Even the empty bag makes up a large part of the weight.
109470.m: The empty bag also counts towards the total weight.

109471.q: Roughly where should the top edge of the screen be?
a: At or just below eye level
At the height of your belly button
109471.e: If the top edge is at or just below eye level, you look slightly downwards. This takes strain off your neck and eyes.
109471.m: Place the screen so that you look slightly down.

109472.q: Roughly how far away from your eyes should a computer screen be?
109472.e: A distance of about an arm's length, that is about 50 to 70 cm, is comfortable for most screens. For large screens it can be more.
109472.m: The screen should be about an arm's length away.

109473.q: What does the 20-20-20 rule for the eyes say?
a: Every 20 minutes, look into the distance for 20 seconds
Drink 20 litres of water a day
Work for 20 minutes, sleep for 20 minutes
Put the screen 20 cm in front of your eyes
109473.e: Every 20 minutes you should look at something about 20 feet (6 m) away for about 20 seconds. This relaxes the eye muscles.
109473.m: Looking into the distance regularly relaxes the eyes.

109474.q: How should a screen be placed in relation to the window?
a: Side on, looking parallel to the window
Directly in front of the window
With its back to the window
It does not matter, light plays no part
109474.e: If you sit side on to the window, there is no glare and no reflections. Light from the front dazzles, and light from behind reflects in the screen.
109474.m: Place the screen side on to the window.

109475.q: Why do the eyes often get dry during long screen work?
109475.e: When you concentrate on a screen, you blink much less often. As a result, the tear film is renewed less and the eyes dry out.
109475.m: Blinking on purpose helps against dry eyes.

109476.q: How should your feet be placed when sitting at a desk?
109476.e: If your feet are flat on the floor, your thighs and lower legs are at about a right angle. If you cannot reach the floor, a footrest helps.
109476.m: When sitting, keep your feet flat on the floor.

109477.q: Which Swiss accident insurance organisation gives recommendations for ergonomic computer workstations?
109477.e: Suva works for safety and health protection at work. Among other things, it publishes checklists for computer workstations.
109477.m: Suva gives information about healthy workplaces.

109478.q: What is important during long screen work?
a: Sitting for hours without a break
Setting the screen as bright as possible
109478.e: Short breaks and changes of position take strain off the back, neck and eyes. It is best to stand up and move about now and then.
109478.m: Short breaks to move do your body and eyes good.

109479.q: How should your forearms be when typing on a keyboard?
a: Roughly level, with elbows at about a right angle
Hanging below the edge of the desk
109479.e: If your forearms are roughly level and your elbows at about a right angle, your shoulders and wrists stay relaxed. The height of the desk should match this.
109479.m: When typing, rest your forearms loosely and level.

109480.q: In which part of the fridge is it best to store raw meat and fish?
a: On the bottom shelf above the vegetable drawer
109480.e: Cold air sinks, so the bottom shelf above the vegetable drawer is usually the coldest. Highly perishable food stays fresh longest there.
109480.m: Raw meat belongs in the coldest part of the fridge.

109481.q: How does nicotine affect the blood vessels?
109481.e: Nicotine makes the blood vessels narrower, so pulse and blood pressure rise. That is why smokers' hands and feet are often cooler.

a: It makes germs that cause disease harmless
109482.e: To disinfect means to reduce germs so much that they can no longer infect anyone. This needs substances such as alcohol that kill germs.
109482.m: Disinfection makes germs that cause disease harmless.

109483.q: In the morning the thermometer shows -6 °C, at midday 9 °C. By how many degrees has it got warmer?
109483.e: The difference is 9 minus (minus 6), which is 9 plus 6 = 15. So it has got 15 degrees warmer.
109483.m: With temperatures below zero, you add on the distance to zero.

109484.q: How many equal parts are there on the Celsius scale between the freezing point and the boiling point of water?
109484.e: Celsius divided the distance between the two fixed points into 100 equal parts. Each part equals one degree Celsius.
109484.m: There are 100 degrees Celsius between freezing point and boiling point.

109485.e: The freezing point of water is 32 °F on the Fahrenheit scale. This comes from 0 · 9/5 + 32 = 32.

109486.e: You calculate 100 · 9/5 + 32 = 180 + 32 = 212. So water boils at 212 °F.

109487.q: At which temperature do the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales show the same value?
109487.e: If you put C = F into F = C · 9/5 + 32, you get C = -40. So -40 °C is exactly -40 °F.
109487.m: At minus 40 degrees, Celsius and Fahrenheit show the same.

109488.q: How do you convert a temperature from degrees Celsius into degrees Fahrenheit?
109488.e: The formula is °F = °C · 1.8 + 32. So one degree Celsius is 1.8 degrees Fahrenheit.
109488.m: For Fahrenheit, multiply by 1.8 and add 32.

109489.m: A room temperature of 20 °C is 68 degrees Fahrenheit.

109490.q: Which measuring instrument did Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit build especially accurately?
109490.e: The physicist Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit built accurate thermometers with mercury. In 1724, he also presented his own temperature scale.
109490.m: Fahrenheit built thermometers and invented the Fahrenheit scale.

109491.e: You calculate T in kelvin = temperature in °C + 273.15. For 0 °C, this gives 273.15 K.
109491.m: The freezing point of water is 273.15 kelvin.

109492.q: Roughly how many degrees Celsius are 0 kelvin, that is absolute zero?
109492.e: The Kelvin scale starts at absolute zero. It is at -273.15 °C, and nothing can be colder.

109493.q: How do you write a temperature in kelvin correctly?
109493.e: With kelvin, you do not write a degree sign. Since 1967, the unit has simply been called “kelvin”, not “degrees Kelvin”.
109493.m: Kelvin is written without a degree sign.

109494.q: How many degrees Celsius are 373.15 K?
109494.e: You calculate 373.15 minus 273.15 = 100. That is the boiling point of water.

109495.q: The temperature rises from 15 °C to 25 °C. By how many kelvin has it risen?
109495.e: One kelvin is the same size as one degree Celsius. A rise of 10 °C is therefore also a rise of 10 K.
109495.m: Temperature differences are the same size in kelvin and degrees Celsius.

109496.q: What is special about the Kelvin scale?
109496.e: The Kelvin scale starts at absolute zero. No temperature can be lower, so there are no negative kelvin values.

109497.q: Which system of units does the kelvin belong to as a base unit?
109497.e: The kelvin is one of the seven base units of the International System of Units. These also include the metre, the kilogram and the second.
109497.m: The kelvin is an SI base unit.

109498.q: What happens to the movement of particles as a substance approaches absolute zero?
109498.e: Temperature is a measure of the movement of particles. At absolute zero, they would have the lowest possible energy.
109498.m: The colder a substance, the less its particles move.

109499.q: Can absolute zero be reached exactly in the laboratory?
a: No, you can only get very close
109499.e: According to the third law of thermodynamics, absolute zero cannot be reached. But researchers get to within billionths of a kelvin of it.
109499.m: Absolute zero can never quite be reached.

109500.q: Roughly how many degrees Celsius is absolute zero?
109500.e: Absolute zero is at -273.15 °C. It cannot get any colder.

109501.q: How cold is it in empty space far away from stars?
a: About as cold as in a freezer
109501.e: Far from stars, space is about -270 °C cold. That is only a little warmer than absolute zero.
109501.m: Space is only a little warmer than absolute zero.

109502.q: Which temperature scale starts at 0 at absolute zero?
109502.e: The Kelvin scale starts at absolute zero. A step of 1 kelvin is the same size as 1 degree Celsius.
109502.m: The Kelvin scale starts at absolute zero.

109503.q: What happens to air if you cool it very strongly?
109503.e: At about -200 °C, the nitrogen and oxygen in the air become liquid. Liquid air is used in industry and research.
109503.m: Gases cooled very strongly become liquid.

109504.q: How does the volume of an ideal gas behave at constant pressure when it is cooled?
a: It first gets bigger, then smaller
109504.e: At constant pressure, the volume of an ideal gas is proportional to its kelvin temperature. If you extend this line downwards, you arrive at absolute zero.
109504.m: A gas contracts when it cools.

109505.q: What happens to most substances when they are heated?
109505.e: When heated, the particles move more and need more space. That is why most substances expand.
109505.m: Heat makes most substances get bigger.

109506.q: Which substances expand the most when heated by the same amount?
109506.e: In gases the particles are hardly bound to each other. That is why gases expand much more than liquids and solids.
109506.m: Gases expand the most when heated.

109507.q: Why do power lines sag lower in summer than in winter?
a: The wires expand in the heat
The pylons sink into the ground
109507.e: Heat makes the wires longer. Because the pylons stay the same distance apart, the longer wires sag lower.
109507.m: In summer power lines get longer and sag lower.

109508.q: A steel rail is 100 m long and expands by 0.012 mm per metre for each kelvin. How much longer does it get when heated by 30 K?
109508.e: You calculate 100 · 0.012 mm · 30 = 36 mm. So the rail gets 3.6 cm longer.
109508.m: The change in length grows with the length and the temperature difference.

109509.q: Why can a thick glass crack when you pour boiling water into it?
a: The inside and outside expand unevenly
109509.e: The inside heats up quickly while the outside is still cool. The uneven expansion creates stresses that can break the glass.
109509.m: Sudden temperature changes can make glass crack.

109510.q: How can you open a stuck metal lid on a jam jar more easily?
a: Warm the lid with warm water
Put the jar in the freezer
109510.e: Metal expands more than glass when heated. The lid becomes slightly wider and is easier to turn.
109510.m: A warm metal lid is easier to open.

109511.q: Why does a hot-air balloon rise?
a: Warm air is less dense than cold air
The basket is as light as air
109511.e: The heated air in the balloon expands and some of it flows out. The air left inside is lighter than the same amount of cold outside air, so there is lift.
109511.m: Warm air rises because it is less dense.

109512.q: Do all substances expand by the same amount when heated equally?
a: No, each substance expands by a different amount
109512.e: Every substance has its own thermal expansion. Aluminium, for example, expands about twice as much as steel.
109512.m: Each substance expands by a different amount.

109513.q: What is a bimetallic strip made of?
109513.e: A bimetallic strip consists of two different metals that are firmly joined together. “Bi” means two.
109513.m: A bimetallic strip is made of two joined metals.

109514.q: Why does a bimetallic strip bend when it is heated?
a: The metals expand by different amounts
109514.e: One metal expands more than the other. Because both are firmly joined, the strip curves.
109514.m: Uneven expansion makes the bimetallic strip bend.

109515.q: Which way does a heated bimetallic strip bend?
a: towards the metal that expands less
towards the metal that expands more
109515.e: The metal that expands more gets longer and lies on the outside of the curve. So the strip bends towards the side of the metal that expands less.
109515.m: The metal that expands more is on the outside of the bend.

109516.q: In which household appliance does a bimetallic strip often switch off the heating when it is hot enough?
109516.e: In an iron, a bimetallic strip bends at the set temperature and opens an electrical contact. When it cools, the contact closes again.
109516.m: A bimetallic strip controls the temperature in an iron.

109517.q: What happens to a bent bimetallic strip when it cools down again?
109517.e: As they cool, both metals contract back to their original length. The strip returns to its original shape.
109517.m: A bimetallic strip returns to its shape when it cools.

109518.q: Why can't you make a bimetallic strip from two strips of the same metal?
a: Both would expand equally and not bend
Identical metals do not conduct electricity
109518.e: A bimetallic strip only bends because the two metals expand by different amounts. With the same metal, the strip would just get longer.
109518.m: A bimetallic strip needs two metals that expand differently.

109519.q: What can a bimetallic strip be used for in a fire alarm?
a: It closes an electric circuit when hot
109519.e: When it gets hot, the strip bends and touches a contact. This closes the circuit and the alarm sounds.
109519.m: A bimetallic strip can set off an alarm when it gets hot.

109520.q: What could happen to a concrete slab without expansion joints on hot days?
109520.e: If the concrete cannot expand, large stresses build up. The slab can then buckle or break.
109520.m: Without expansion joints, stresses cause cracks.

109521.q: Why do you often feel a small bump when a car drives onto a bridge?
a: There is an expansion joint with a metal cover
The tyres get colder on the bridge
109521.e: Bridges expand in the heat. So at the end there is a gap covered by a metal joint. You feel a short rumble as you drive over it.
109521.m: There is an expansion joint at the end of a bridge.

109522.q: How do we stop welded railway tracks from buckling in the heat today?
a: They are firmly anchored to sleepers and pre-stressed
109522.e: Continuously welded rails are firmly anchored to sleepers and in the ballast. The stress in the steel is absorbed instead of bending the rail.
109522.m: Modern rails are firmly anchored without gaps.

109523.q: Why did you use to hear a regular “clickety-clack” on train journeys?
a: Because of the gaps between the rail sections
109523.e: In the past, rails were laid in short sections with small gaps for thermal expansion. The wheels knocked at every gap.
109523.m: Gaps in the rails left room for thermal expansion.

109524.q: What are expansion joints in buildings often filled with?
109524.e: Elastic sealants can be squeezed and stretched. This keeps the joint sealed while still allowing movement.
109524.m: Joints are filled with elastic material.

109525.q: Why does the liquid in a thermometer rise when it gets warmer?
109525.e: When warm, the liquid in the bulb expands. It only has room in the thin tube, so it rises.
109525.m: The liquid in a thermometer rises because it expands.

109526.q: What is the very thin tube in a liquid thermometer called?
109526.e: The capillary is a hair-thin glass tube. Because it is so thin, even a small expansion makes the liquid rise clearly.
109526.m: A thermometer shows temperature in a thin capillary.

109527.q: Which liquid is used in many thermometers with red or blue colour?
109527.e: Many thermometers contain coloured alcohol because it is easy to see and less poisonous than mercury. It also only freezes at very low temperatures.
109527.m: Red thermometer liquid is usually coloured alcohol.

109528.q: Why is a mercury thermometer unsuitable for temperatures below about -39 °C?
109528.e: Mercury solidifies at about -38.8 °C. That is why alcohol thermometers are used for very low temperatures.
109528.m: Mercury freezes at about minus 39 degrees.

109529.q: Why have mercury thermometers largely been replaced?
109529.e: If a mercury thermometer breaks, poisonous vapours can form. Today mainly alcohol or digital thermometers are used.
109529.m: Mercury is poisonous, so it is hardly used any more.

109530.q: What is the narrow part in the tube of a classic clinical thermometer for?
109530.e: The narrowing stops the liquid from flowing straight back after measuring. So you can read the highest value calmly and then have to shake the thermometer down.
109530.m: A clinical thermometer holds the highest reading.

109531.q: Which scientist built a thermoscope, an early form of the thermometer, around 1600?
109531.e: Around 1600 Galileo Galilei developed a thermoscope with an air bubble above water. It showed changes in temperature but had no scale yet.
109531.m: Galileo Galilei built an early form of the thermometer.

109532.q: What was Anders Celsius mainly by profession?
109532.e: Celsius was professor of astronomy at Uppsala University. He also founded an observatory there.

109533.q: Which two points of water did Celsius use for his temperature scale?
109533.e: Celsius divided the range between the freezing point and boiling point of water into 100 equal parts.
109533.m: The Celsius scale is based on the freezing and boiling points of water.

109534.q: How was Anders Celsius's original scale different from today's?
a: It was the other way round
It used milk instead of water
109534.e: Celsius set the boiling point at 0 and the freezing point at 100. Shortly after his death the scale was reversed.
109534.m: The first Celsius scale was upside down.

109536.q: Which phenomenon in the sky did Anders Celsius study and link to the Earth's magnetic field?
109536.e: With his assistant, Celsius observed that the compass needle moves during the northern lights. So he recognised a link with the Earth's magnetic field.
109536.m: Celsius linked the northern lights to the Earth's magnetism.

109537.q: Into how many parts is the Celsius scale divided between the freezing and boiling points of water?
109537.e: The freezing point is at 0 °C, the boiling point at 100 °C. In between are 100 equal degrees.
109537.m: There are 100 degrees Celsius between freezing and boiling.

109538.e: A thermostat compares the measured temperature with the set value. It switches heating or cooling on or off until the value is reached.
109538.m: A thermostat controls the temperature by itself.

109539.q: What do you call the temperature you set on a thermostat?
109539.e: The set point is the temperature you want. The actual value is the temperature really measured.
109539.m: On a thermostat you set the set point.

109540.q: On many radiator thermostats, roughly what room temperature does setting 3 correspond to?
109540.e: On many thermostatic valves, setting 3 stands for around 20 °C. Each setting up or down changes the temperature by a few degrees.
109540.m: Setting 3 on a radiator usually means about 20 °C.

109541.q: Roughly how much heating energy do you save by lowering the room temperature by 1 °C?
109541.e: As a rule of thumb, each degree less saves around 6 per cent of heating energy. That is why it pays not to overheat.
109541.m: One degree less saves about six per cent of heating energy.

109542.q: Which component is found in many thermostatic radiator valves?
109542.e: The expansion element contains wax, a liquid or a gas that expands when warm. It then pushes the valve shut and reduces the flow of hot water.
109542.m: An expansion element controls many radiator valves.

109543.q: Why shouldn't you cover a radiator thermostat with furniture or curtains?
a: Otherwise it measures the wrong temperature
109543.e: Heat builds up behind curtains. The thermostat then measures a higher temperature than in the room and turns the heating down too early.
109543.m: A thermostat needs free air to measure correctly.

109544.q: In which appliance does a thermostat keep the inside temperature low?
109544.e: In a fridge the thermostat switches on the compressor when it gets too warm. When the desired cold is reached, it switches it off again.
109544.m: A thermostat switches the fridge on and off.

109545.q: Roughly what temperature is the water at the bottom of a deep, frozen lake?
109545.e: Water at 4 °C has the highest density and so sinks to the bottom. There it stays liquid even in winter, so fish can survive.
109545.m: At the bottom of frozen lakes the water is about 4 °C.

109546.q: By roughly how much does the volume increase when water freezes into ice?
109546.e: When freezing, water expands by around 9 per cent. That is why a completely full glass bottle can burst in the freezer.
109546.m: As ice, water needs about nine per cent more space.

109547.q: What is it called when freezing water in cracks breaks rocks apart?
109547.e: Water gets into cracks in the rock and expands when it freezes. If this happens often, the rock breaks apart, as you can see in the Alps.
109547.m: Frost shattering breaks up rocks in the mountains.

109548.q: In which direction does a lake freeze in winter?
109548.e: Because of the anomaly, the coldest water stays at the top. So the ice forms first at the surface.

109549.q: How does the volume of water change when you cool it from 4 °C to 1 °C?
109549.e: Below 4 °C water expands again as it cools. This behaviour is called the anomaly of water.
109549.m: Below four degrees water expands as it cools.

109550.q: What does a gas thermometer measure to find the temperature?
a: the pressure or volume of a gas
109550.e: In a gas thermometer, the pressure or volume of a trapped amount of gas changes with temperature. From this the temperature is calculated.
109550.m: A gas thermometer uses the pressure or volume of a gas.

109551.q: Which gases are especially good for gas thermometers?
109551.e: Helium and hydrogen behave almost like ideal gases down to very low temperatures. They only become liquid very late.
109551.m: Helium is good for gas thermometers.

109553.q: What happens to a blown-up balloon if you put it in the fridge?
109553.e: Cold air takes up less space than warm air. So the air in the balloon contracts and the balloon gets smaller.

109554.q: At constant pressure, by what fraction of its volume at 0 °C does an ideal gas expand per degree of heating?
109554.e: An ideal gas expands by about 1/273 of its volume at 0 °C per kelvin. This observation led to the idea of absolute zero.
109554.m: Gases expand by about one 273rd per degree.

109555.q: Why does a football get harder when it lies in the sun for a long time?
a: The air inside warms up and pushes harder
The sun pumps air into it
The leather shrinks in the sun
109555.e: Warm gas particles move faster and hit the casing harder. The pressure in the ball rises.

109556.q: What happens to the pressure of a gas in a closed container when you heat it?
109556.e: When warm, the gas particles move faster and hit the wall more often and harder. This raises the pressure.

109557.e: Below zero, the closer the value is to zero, the warmer it is. -5 °C is closest to zero and so the warmest.
109557.m: Below zero, the temperature closest to zero is the warmest.

109558.q: It is 3 °C, then the temperature drops by 8 degrees. How cold is it now?
109558.e: You calculate 3 − 8 = -5. The temperature is now 5 degrees below zero.
109558.m: When the temperature drops below zero, it becomes negative.

109559.q: On three days the readings are -2 °C, 4 °C and 7 °C. What is the average?
109559.e: You add them up and divide by 3: (-2 + 4 + 7) ÷ 3 = 9 ÷ 3 = 3. The average is 3 °C.
109559.m: You get the average by dividing the total by the number of values.

109560.q: What is the difference between -12 °C and -3 °C?
109560.e: You calculate -3 − (-12) = -3 + 12 = 9. The difference is 9 degrees.
109560.m: Between two temperatures below zero, the distance counts too.

109561.m: For Celsius, subtract 32 and divide by 1.8.

109562.q: Which value in degrees Fahrenheit matches the normal body temperature of 37 °C?
109562.e: You calculate 37 · 1.8 + 32 = 66.6 + 32 = 98.6. In the USA, 98.6 °F is considered normal body temperature.

109563.q: At how many degrees Fahrenheit does water freeze?
109563.e: 0 °C equals 0 · 1.8 + 32 = 32 °F. So the zero of the Fahrenheit scale is not at the freezing point of water.

109564.q: How many kelvin is -73 °C if you use 273?
109564.e: You calculate -73 + 273 = 200. So -73 °C is about 200 K.
109564.m: Even minus degrees become positive numbers in kelvin.

109565.q: What do you call a temperature given in kelvin?
109565.e: The kelvin scale starts at absolute zero. That is why a temperature in kelvin is also called absolute temperature.
109565.m: Kelvin values are called absolute temperatures.

109566.q: Which of these temperatures is physically impossible?
109566.e: Absolute zero is at -273.15 °C; it can't get any lower. So a temperature of -300 °C is impossible.
109566.m: No temperature is below absolute zero.

109567.q: Apart from bridges, where else are expansion joints often found?
109567.e: Large concrete areas such as car parks, hall floors or pavements are divided into sections by joints. This lets the slabs expand in the heat without cracking.
109567.m: Large concrete areas need expansion joints.

109568.q: Why does a long bridge need wider expansion joints than a short one?
109568.e: The change in length is proportional to the length. A bridge twice as long expands twice as much when heated by the same amount.
109568.m: The longer a part, the more it expands.

109569.q: A steel bridge is 500 m long. Steel expands by 0.012 mm per metre per kelvin. How much longer does it get when heated by 40 K?
109569.e: You calculate 500 · 0.012 mm · 40 = 240 mm. So the bridge gets 24 cm longer.
109569.m: Large structures expand by many centimetres.

109570.q: Why aren't drinks bottles filled right to the top?
a: The liquid needs room to expand
109570.e: When warm, the liquid expands. The empty space stops the bottle from leaking or bursting because of too much pressure.
109570.m: Bottles need air at the top so the contents can expand.

109571.q: Why does the pressure in a bicycle tyre rise when the bike stands in the hot sun?
a: The air in the tyre warms up
109571.e: Warm air wants to expand, but the tyre leaves little room. So the pressure in the tyre rises.
109571.m: In the heat the pressure in a tyre rises.

109572.q: Why doesn't a good glass baking dish crack in a hot oven?
a: Its glass expands only a little when heated
Its glass is filled with water
109572.e: Baking dishes and lab vessels are often made of borosilicate glass. It hardly expands, so only small stresses arise when the temperature changes.
109572.m: Special glass copes well with temperature changes.

109573.q: Why does ice float on water?
a: Ice is less dense than water
109573.e: Water expands when it freezes. So ice is slightly less dense than liquid water and floats on top.
109573.m: Ice is less dense than water and floats.

109574.q: What protects the water under a layer of ice from cooling further?
a: The ice acts as an insulating layer
109574.e: Ice conducts heat poorly and sits on the water like a lid. So the water beneath cools only slowly.
109574.m: A layer of ice insulates the water below.

109575.q: Roughly what part of an iceberg sticks out of the sea?
109575.e: Ice is only slightly less dense than seawater. That is why about 90 per cent of an iceberg lies below the surface.
109575.m: You only see the tip of the iceberg.

109576.q: Why do people drain the water pipes in a holiday home before winter?
a: Freezing water expands and can burst the pipes
109576.e: Water expands when it freezes. In a full pipe this creates so much pressure that the pipe can burst.

109577.q: In which country is everyday temperature mostly measured in Fahrenheit instead of Celsius?
109577.e: Almost all countries use degrees Celsius today. In the USA, however, the Fahrenheit scale is still common in everyday life.
109577.m: Almost the whole world measures in degrees Celsius.

109578.q: Which measuring device shows the temperature with a coiled bimetallic spiral?
109578.e: The bimetallic spiral winds up or unwinds with heat and turns a pointer. Such thermometers are often found on ovens or house walls.
109578.m: A bimetallic spiral can move a thermometer pointer.

109579.q: Which temperature scale can be measured most directly with a gas thermometer?
109579.e: At constant volume, gas pressure is proportional to the absolute temperature. So a gas thermometer measures temperatures directly in kelvin.

109580.q: What does a maximum-minimum thermometer show?
a: the lowest and highest temperature since it was reset
the air pressure of the day
109580.e: Small markers stay at the lowest and highest point reached. Gardeners use such thermometers to detect frost at night.
109580.m: A max-min thermometer remembers the extreme values.

109581.q: What does night setback mean for heating?
a: The room temperature is set lower at night
The heating runs harder at night
109581.e: With night setback, the controller automatically lowers the set point at night. This saves energy while you sleep.
109581.m: At night the flat can be a little cooler.

109582.q: How does a cushion plant grow in the high mountains?
a: Very dense and flat, as a round dome
Tall and slim like a small tree
As a climbing plant up rocks
109582.e: Cushion plants form lots of short shoots packed tightly together. This creates a dense, domed cushion that rises only a little above the ground.
109582.m: Cushion plants grow tightly packed and flat on the ground.

109583.q: Why is it often warmer inside a plant cushion than in the surroundings?
a: The dense cushion keeps out the wind and stores heat
The plant makes fire with its roots
Warm animals always live in the cushion
The cushion always lies over hot springs
109583.e: Between the tightly packed shoots, the air hardly moves. The sun warms the cushion, and the heat stays stored in it for a long time.
109583.m: A dense cushion protects the plant from wind and cold.

109584.q: Which alpine plant is a typical example of a cushion plant?
109584.e: Moss campion forms flat cushions with pink flowers on rocks and scree. Gentian, alder and larch do not grow as dense cushions.
109584.m: Moss campion is a well-known cushion plant of the Alps.

109585.q: What happens to the dead leaves inside a plant cushion?
a: They stay inside and store water and nutrients
They are blown away by the wind at once
The plant pushes them out and buries them
109585.e: The old leaves rot slowly in the cushion. Like a sponge, they hold on to moisture and provide the plant with nutrients.
109585.m: In a cushion, old leaves act as the plant's own store of water and nutrients.

109586.q: What is the advantage of a cushion's round, flat shape in a storm?
a: The wind drives the plant down the valley
The plant can turn in the wind
The leaves get brushed by the wind
109586.e: A low, domed shape gives the wind hardly anything to push against. The plant is neither bent nor dried out.
109586.m: Flat cushions give the wind hardly anything to push against.

109587.q: Up to what height do cushion plants such as purple saxifrage grow in the Alps?
109587.e: Purple saxifrage forms low cushions with violet flowers. In the Valais Alps it has been found at over 4000 metres.
109587.m: Cushion plants grow at extreme heights.

109588.q: Why do cushion plants grow only very slowly?
a: Cold and short summers slow down their growth
They get too much fertiliser in the mountains
They have no leaves for photosynthesis
109588.e: In the high mountains there is only a short warm period each year for growing. A large cushion can therefore be many decades old.
109588.m: Large cushion plants are often many decades old.

109589.q: Why should you not step on plant cushions in the mountains?
a: They grow back only very slowly after damage
They contain a strong poison for the skin
They are especially slippery, like ice
109589.e: Because of the short summers, a trampled cushion takes a very long time to recover. Staying on the paths protects the plants.
109589.m: Staying on the paths protects delicate alpine plants.

109590.q: Why does your skin sting when you touch a stinging nettle?
a: Fine stinging hairs break off and release a liquid
The plant bites with tiny teeth
The leaves are full of sand
109590.e: The stinging nettle has fine hairs with a fragile tip. When touched, the tip breaks off and a stinging liquid gets into the skin.
109590.m: Stinging nettles protect themselves with stinging hairs.

109591.q: Which well-known alpine flower is covered in thick, white woolly hairs?
109591.e: Edelweiss is covered with a thick felt of white hairs. This fur protects the plant from cold, drying out and strong sunshine.
109591.m: Edelweiss wears a coat of white hair for protection.

109592.q: Why do thickly hairy parts of plants often look silvery or white?
a: Air between the hairs reflects the light
The hairs are filled with snow
The plant stores lime in its hairs
The hairs are made of fine metal
109592.e: Many plant hairs are dead cells filled with air. They scatter and reflect the light, which is why they look white.
109592.m: Air-filled plant hairs reflect a lot of light and look white.

109593.q: How does thick hair protect a leaf from drying out?
a: It keeps a still, moist layer of air on the leaf
It sucks water from the air like a pipe
It seals all the plant's roots
109593.e: Between the hairs, the air hardly moves. This means the wind cannot carry the moisture away from the leaf so quickly.
109593.m: Plant hairs slow down the evaporation of water.

109594.q: What protection against the high mountain sun do pale plant hairs give?
a: They block some of the UV rays
They strengthen the UV rays in the leaf
They make the plant invisible to insects
They direct lightning into the ground
109594.e: The hairs work like a sunshade. They scatter some of the light and UV radiation before it reaches the leaf cells.
109594.m: Pale plant hairs work like sun protection.

109595.q: Why do some alpine flowers already wear a furry coat of hair in spring?
a: It protects them from the cold
109595.e: Many alpine flowers, such as the spring pasque flower, bloom soon after the snow melts. Their coat of hair holds a layer of air and so protects them from the cold.
109595.m: A coat of hair protects alpine flowers from the cold.

109596.q: How do hairs protect a plant on cold mountain nights?
a: Like a jumper, they keep the warmth in
They make heat themselves by rubbing
They quickly carry heat away into the air
They draw warm water from the ground
109596.e: Air does not conduct heat well. The layer of air between the hairs insulates the plant like a woolly jumper.
109596.m: Plant hairs insulate like a warm jumper.

109597.q: What are the white, hairy rays that form a star on edelweiss?
a: Seeds that will soon fly away
109597.e: The white rays are hairy bracts, not petals. The real, tiny flowers sit in the yellowish heads in the middle.
109597.m: On edelweiss, hairy bracts form the white star.

109598.q: What is typical of a rosette plant?
a: Its leaves lie in a circle close to the ground
Its leaves only grow at the tip of the stem
It has no leaves at all
Its leaves hang down like lianas
109598.e: In a rosette, all the leaves come from almost the same place. They spread out flat over the ground like a star.
109598.m: Rosette plants hold their leaves in a star shape close to the ground.

109599.q: Which plant forms thick, fleshy rosettes of leaves and often grows on rocks and walls?
109599.e: The houseleek forms round rosettes of thick leaves. In them it stores water for dry spells on bare rock.
109599.m: The houseleek stores water in its thick rosette leaves.

109600.q: Why is growing close to the ground good for rosette plants in the mountains?
a: It is warmer and less windy near the ground
There is more sunlight near the ground than higher up
Animals do not eat plants near the ground
Snow never falls near the ground
109600.e: The ground stores the warmth of the day, and the wind is weaker there. This way the flat leaves benefit from a milder small-scale climate.
109600.m: Close to the ground the climate is milder for plants.

109601.q: How did the cobweb houseleek get its name?
a: Fine white hairs join the tips of the leaves
It is often eaten by spiders
It only grows in old spider webs
109601.e: Fine white hairs stretch between the tips of the leaves. They look like a spider web over the rosette.
109601.m: The cobweb houseleek is covered with fine hairs like a web.

109602.q: What happens to a houseleek rosette after it has flowered?
a: It dies, but its baby rosettes live on
It flowers again every year after that
109602.e: A houseleek rosette flowers only once and then dies. But the many small baby rosettes around it keep growing.
109602.m: Each houseleek rosette flowers only once in its life.

109603.q: Which well-known meadow plant from the lowlands also grows as a rosette?
109603.e: All the leaves of a dandelion grow from one point close to the ground. Sunflowers, maize and hops have tall, leafy stems.
109603.m: The dandelion is a rosette plant too.

109604.q: How does the snow cover help flat rosette plants in winter?
a: The snow covers them and protects them from frost
The snow presses the leaves into the earth
The snow gives them a lot of light
The snow fertilises them with salt
109604.e: A layer of snow insulates well, and underneath it stays around freezing point. Flat rosettes under it are protected from icy winds and hard frost.
109604.m: Under the snow, flat plants are protected from hard frost.

109605.q: Why did people in the past like to plant houseleeks on roofs?
a: An old folk belief said they protected against lightning
They kept rainwater away from the house
They were used as food for hens
They warmed the roof in winter
109605.e: In folk belief, the houseleek protected a house from lightning strikes. That is also where names such as the German ‘Dachwurz’ (roof root) come from.
109605.m: The houseleek was once thought to protect against lightning.

109606.q: Roughly how long is the growing season for plants in the alpine zone?
109606.e: In the high mountains snow lies for a long time and frost returns early. Only a short summer is left for growing, flowering and making seeds.
109606.m: In the high mountains, plants have only a short summer to grow.

109607.q: What is the time of year called when plants can grow and flower?
109607.e: The growing season is the time with enough warmth and light for plants to grow. In the mountains it is much shorter than on the Central Plateau.
109607.m: The time when plants grow is called the growing season.

109608.q: Why are almost all high mountain plants perennial and not annual?
a: One summer is often not enough to go from seed to seed
Annual plants are banned in the Alps
Perennial plants do not need light
Annual plants freeze while still seeds
109608.e: An annual plant has to sprout, grow, flower and make seeds in one summer. This rarely works in the short mountain summer, so most alpine plants live for many years.

109609.q: How do many alpine plants manage to flower right after the snow melts?
a: They form their flower buds the year before
They flower under the snow in winter
They take flowers from other plants
They wait three years for warm weather
109609.e: Many alpine plants form their buds in the late summer before. In spring they only have to open them, which saves valuable time.
109609.m: Many alpine plants form their flower buds the year before.

109610.q: On average, by roughly how much does the air temperature drop for every 100 metres you climb?
109610.e: As you go higher, the air gets cooler by about half to two thirds of a degree per 100 metres on average. That is why summer is shorter and colder higher up.
109610.m: The higher you climb, the colder it gets.

109611.q: Where do many alpine plants store reserves so that they can sprout quickly in spring?
a: In the seeds of other plants
In the snow around the plant
109611.e: In late summer, many alpine plants store sugar and starch in their roots or rootstocks. This lets them start growing straight away in spring.
109611.m: Alpine plants store supplies for spring in their roots.

109612.q: Which way of reproducing is especially common in alpine plants because of the short summer?
a: Reproducing only through the fruits of trees
Reproducing only with the help of birds
109612.e: In the high mountains it is uncertain whether enough seeds will ripen. That is why many plants also form runners, buds that grow into new plants, or offshoots.
109612.m: Many alpine plants also reproduce through runners and offshoots.

109613.q: How does UV radiation change as you climb higher into the mountains?
109613.e: The higher you are, the less air there is above you to block UV rays. UV radiation increases by about 10 percent for every 1000 metres of height.
109613.m: In the mountains, UV radiation is stronger than in the valley.

109614.q: Why is UV exposure especially high on a snowfield?
a: The snow reflects a lot of UV radiation
The snow produces UV radiation itself
There are no clouds over snow
109614.e: Fresh snow reflects a large part of the UV radiation. You then get the rays from above and from below as well.
109614.m: Snow reflects UV radiation and so increases its effect.

109615.q: Which pigments do many alpine plants produce to protect themselves from strong UV radiation?
109615.e: Anthocyanins colour leaves and flowers red, purple or blue. In the outer layers of cells they work like sun cream.
109615.m: Anthocyanins protect plants like sun cream.

109616.q: Why are the flowers of many mountain plants especially brightly coloured?
a: Lots of pigment protects against UV and attracts insects
The cold air colours the flowers automatically
The snow colours the flowers as it melts
109616.e: Pigments protect plant tissue from too much UV radiation. At the same time, bright flowers are easier for the few pollinators in the mountains to spot.
109616.m: Bright flower colours help against UV rays and attract pollinators.

109617.q: Why does more UV radiation reach the ground at high altitude than in the valley?
a: The layer of air above is thinner
The sun is closer to the Earth there
There are more suns in the mountains
109617.e: The atmosphere absorbs some of the UV radiation. On top of a mountain the layer of air is thinner, so it filters out less.
109617.m: Thinner air filters out less UV radiation.

109618.q: Which layer of a plant is the first to protect the inside of a leaf from UV rays?
a: The outer skin with wax and pigments
109618.e: The outer skin of the leaf contains protective substances and is often coated with a layer of wax. It blocks a large part of the UV rays before they reach the inside of the leaf.
109618.m: The outer skin protects the inside of the leaf from UV radiation.

109619.q: What can too much UV radiation damage in plant cells?
a: The genetic material and the chlorophyll
Only the colour of the roots
Only the scent of the flowers
109619.e: Strong UV radiation can damage the genetic material and the chlorophyll in the cells. That is why high mountain plants need special protective substances.
109619.m: UV radiation can damage plants' genetic material and chlorophyll.

109620.q: Which protection against UV radiation is most important for people on mountain walks?
a: Sun cream, sunglasses and a hat
Lots of salt in the picnic
109620.e: Like plants, people at high altitude need protection from UV radiation. Sun cream, sunglasses and a hat prevent sunburn and eye damage.
109620.m: In the mountains you need especially good sun protection.

a: A hollow where the snow lies for an especially long time
A valley where it never snows
109621.e: In such hollows and dips, the snow only melts in midsummer. The plants there have an extremely short growing season.
109621.m: In snowbeds, the snow stays well into the summer.

109622.q: Which dwarf shrub of snowbeds is thought to be one of the smallest trees in the world?
109622.e: The dwarf willow is a woody plant whose tiny trunks creep in the ground. Only a few centimetres with small, round leaves stick out above the earth.
109622.m: The dwarf willow is a tiny tree of the snowbeds.

109623.q: Which group of plants is especially common in snowbeds that are covered in snow for a very long time?
109623.e: Mosses cope well with a very short growing season and lots of wetness. In the hollows that stay snowy the longest, they often make up most of the plant cover.
109623.m: Mosses grow well in hollows that stay snowy for a long time.

109624.q: Which alpine flower can melt its way through the last snow with its flowers?
109624.e: When they sprout, alpine snowbells produce a little heat by breathing. This lets them melt small holes in the thin layer of snow and flower while still in the snow.
109624.m: Alpine snowbells can melt their way through thin snow.

109625.q: Roughly how long does snow lie in typical snowbeds?
a: About nine to ten months a year
109625.e: In snowbeds, the snow only melts in July or August. The plants often have only about two months without snow cover.
109625.m: In snowbeds, plants have only a few weeks without snow.

109626.q: Why is there much more snow in a snowbed than on the slopes around it?
a: The wind blows extra snow into the hollow
Snow only falls there at night
109626.e: The wind carries snow from hilltops and ridges and drops it in sheltered hollows. There the snow cover becomes especially thick and melts late.
109626.m: Snow blown by the wind piles up especially high in hollows.

109627.q: What is the ground in a snowbed usually like in summer?
a: Damp for a long time from meltwater
109627.e: The melting snow soaks the ground in the hollow. That is why it is usually damp and cool there in summer.
109627.m: Meltwater keeps the ground in snowbeds damp.

109628.q: Why do plants in a snowbed usually stay very small?
a: They have only a few weeks to grow
109628.e: The short time without snow is only enough for a little growth. That is why the plants there are tiny and grow close to the ground.
109628.m: Little time to grow keeps the plants in snowbeds small.

109629.q: Which dwarf shrub turns whole mountainsides bright red in early summer?
109629.e: The alpenrose is an evergreen dwarf shrub with red flowers. It often grows in large patches at the tree line and above.
109629.m: In early summer, the alpenrose turns whole slopes red.

109630.q: Which kind of plant cover is typical of the alpine zone?
109630.e: Above the tree line, low grassland made of grasses, sedges and flowers grows. There are also small shrubs such as alpenroses.
109630.m: In the alpine zone, mainly grassland and low shrubs grow.

109631.q: Which bird of the alpine zone has snow-white feathers in winter?
109631.e: The rock ptarmigan changes its feathers with the seasons. In winter it is white and well camouflaged in the snow.
109631.m: The rock ptarmigan is as white as snow in winter.

109632.q: Which yellow-flowered medicinal plant grows in poor mountain meadows and is used in creams for bruises?
109632.e: Arnica grows in mountain meadows that are poor in nutrients. Creams and tinctures for bumps and bruises are made from its flowers.
109632.m: Arnica is a medicinal plant of mountain meadows.

109633.q: Which animal typically lives in the grassland of the alpine zone and gives a warning whistle?
109633.e: Marmots dig their burrows in alpine meadows. When there is danger, they give loud warning whistles.
109633.m: The marmot lives in the meadows of the alpine zone.

109634.q: Why do trees no longer grow in the alpine zone?
a: The summer is too short and too cool
The ground is too warm there
Trees are always cut down there
There is too much rainforest there
109634.e: Trees need enough warmth for their new shoots to turn woody before winter. Above the tree line, the warm period is no longer long enough for this.
109634.m: Above the tree line, summer is too short for trees.

109635.q: Which flower with deep blue bell-shaped flowers is a well-known symbol of alpine meadows?
109635.e: The trumpet gentian has large, deep blue flowers close to the ground. It grows on alpine pastures and grassland.
109635.m: The blue gentian is a symbol of alpine meadows.

109636.q: What are many areas of the alpine zone in Switzerland used for in summer?
a: As alpine pastures for cows, sheep and goats
109636.e: In summer, cows, sheep and goats graze on the alpine pastures. This alpine farming has a long tradition in Switzerland.
109636.m: Many alpine grasslands are used as summer pastures.

109637.q: What is typical of the nival zone in the high mountains?
a: Lots of snow and ice all year round
109637.e: The word nival comes from the Latin word for snow. In this zone above the snow line, most of the snow stays all year.
109637.m: In the nival zone, snow and ice rule.

109638.q: Where do single flowering plants still grow in the nival zone?
a: In sheltered cracks in rocks and on ridges
In the middle of the glacier ice
At the bottom of deep crevasses
Only in greenhouses at mountain huts
109638.e: Where the wind blows the snow away or rocks store heat, it is free of snow for a short time. Single plants can survive in such cracks and nooks.
109638.m: In the nival zone, plants only survive in sheltered nooks.

109639.q: Which flowering plant is especially typical of the nival zone?
109639.e: The glacier buttercup grows among rocks and scree near glaciers. In the Alps it has been found at over 4000 metres.
109639.m: The glacier buttercup still flowers in the snow zone.

109640.q: Which living things are often the first to settle on the bare rock of the nival zone?
109640.e: Lichens can stand cold, dryness and strong radiation. They cover even high rocks with colourful crusts.
109640.m: Lichens survive even on rocks in the eternal snow.

109641.q: Which tiny animal lives on glaciers and snowfields in the nival zone?
109641.e: The glacier flea is a springtail only about two millimetres long. It lives on ice and snow and eats pollen and dust blown in by the wind.
109641.m: The glacier flea even lives on the ice of glaciers.

109642.q: Roughly at what height does the nival zone begin in the Swiss Alps?
109642.e: Depending on the region, the snow line in the Alps lies at about 2800 to 3200 metres. Above it comes the zone of snow and ice.
109642.m: The nival zone in the Alps begins at around 3000 metres.

109643.q: Why are rocks without snow important for plants in the nival zone?
a: Dark rock warms up in the sun
Rock contains plenty of liquid water
109643.e: Dark rock surfaces absorb the sun's warmth and give it off to their surroundings. Plants in cracks benefit from this.
109643.m: Sun-warmed rock gives plants in the high mountains warmth.

a: The transition area below the snow zone
109644.e: The subnival zone lies between the alpine zone and the nival zone. There are only patchy plants growing among scree and rock there.
109644.m: The subnival zone is the transition from grassland to the snow region.

a: The area uncovered by a retreating glacier
A ski slope right next to the glacier
The highest peak above a glacier
109645.e: When a glacier melts and becomes shorter, rubble and rock are left in front of it. This new land is called a glacier forefield.
109645.m: A glacier forefield forms when a glacier retreats.

109646.q: What are the ridges of rubble that a glacier pushes up and leaves behind called?
109646.e: A glacier carries stones and sand. It drops this rubble at its sides and at its front as moraines.
109646.m: Moraines are ridges of rubble left behind by a glacier.

109647.q: Since when have the Alpine glaciers been retreating especially clearly?
a: Since about the middle of the 19th century
Since the time of the dinosaurs
109647.e: Around 1850, the so-called Little Ice Age ended, when the glaciers were very large. Since then they have shrunk a lot and uncovered large forefields.
109647.m: Since about 1850, the Alpine glaciers have been shrinking a lot.

109648.q: Which living things are the first to settle on the bare rubble of a glacier forefield?
a: Lichens, mosses and small pioneer plants
109648.e: On fresh rock there is no soil yet. First, undemanding lichens, mosses and pioneer plants grow; shrubs and trees only follow much later.
109648.m: Pioneer plants are the first to settle on new land.

109649.q: Where in a glacier forefield do you find the most and the biggest plants?
a: Far away from today's edge of the glacier
Right at today's edge of the ice
In the middle of the glacier streams
109649.e: Places far from the ice were uncovered a long time ago. Plants there have had lots of time to build soil and spread.
109649.m: The longer an area has been free of ice, the thicker the plant growth.

109650.q: What does the fresh ground right in front of the glacier almost completely lack?
109650.e: Humus only forms when dead plants and animals break down. On freshly uncovered rubble there is hardly any yet.
109650.m: Fresh glacier rubble hardly contains any humus.

109651.q: What do signs with dates along the path in front of some glaciers show?
a: Where the ice ended in earlier years
109651.e: At the Morteratsch Glacier in the Upper Engadine, such signs mark the earlier positions of the glacier's tongue. This lets you see the retreat directly in the landscape.
109651.m: Signs in front of glaciers show how far the ice has retreated.

109652.q: Why are researchers especially interested in glacier forefields?
a: You can watch life conquering new land there
Many dinosaur bones are found there
109652.e: In a forefield, areas that have been free of ice for different lengths of time lie next to each other. This makes it possible to compare how soil and plants develop over many decades.
109652.m: Glacier forefields show how life settles on new land.

a: A plant that is the first to settle on new, poor ground
A plant that only grows in gardens
A plant that is the last to grow in a forest
A plant that only lives in water
109653.e: Pioneer plants are the first settlers. They grow on rubble, sand or rock where there is hardly any soil yet.
109653.m: Pioneer plants are the first settlers on poor ground.

109654.q: How do the seeds of many pioneer plants get into a glacier forefield?
a: Light seeds fly on the wind
They grow out of the ice
109654.e: Many pioneer plants have tiny seeds with flying hairs. The wind carries them far across rubble and moraines.
109654.m: The wind brings the seeds of many pioneer plants.

109655.q: Which plant with pink flowers is a typical pioneer plant on glacier rubble and river gravel?
109655.e: Fleischer's willowherb grows on gravel banks and moraines. Its seeds can fly and quickly reach new areas of rubble.
109655.m: Fleischer's willowherb settles on fresh glacier rubble.

109656.q: How do pioneer plants change the place where they grow over time?
a: They form humus and make room for other species
109656.e: When pioneer plants die, humus slowly forms. This soil allows other plants to grow, which often push out the pioneers later.
109656.m: Pioneer plants prepare the ground for later plants.

109657.q: Which mountain shrub takes nitrogen from the air with the help of bacteria on its roots?
109657.e: The green alder lives together with bacteria in small root nodules. These take nitrogen from the air and so also fertilise the poor soil.
109657.m: The green alder fertilises the soil with nitrogen from the air.

109658.q: What do pioneer plants do with their roots in loose rubble?
a: They hold the rubble in place
They loosen it until it slides away
109658.e: The roots spread through gravel and sand. This holds the loose ground together and protects it from being washed away.
109658.m: The roots of pioneer plants hold loose rubble together.

109659.q: Where do pioneer plants typically grow in the Alps?
a: On fresh rubble in front of the glacier
109659.e: Where a glacier retreats, bare rubble is left behind. Pioneer plants are the first to settle on these areas.
109659.m: Pioneer plants settle on fresh glacier rubble.

109660.q: What is typical of many pioneer plants compared with later species?
a: They need a lot of light and few nutrients
They only grow on rich humus
They only sprout under large trees
109660.e: On open areas of rubble there is lots of light but hardly any nutrients. Pioneer plants are adapted to exactly this and are pushed out later in the shade.
109660.m: Pioneer plants love light and make do with few nutrients.

a: Low, crooked woody plants at the tree line
Firewood that bends as it dries
Trees with straight trunks on the Central Plateau
109661.e: In krummholz, trees and shrubs grow lying down and bent. Snow, wind and cold do not allow straight trunks.
109661.m: Krummholz is low, bent woody growth at the tree line.

109662.q: What mainly bends the trunks in krummholz downwards?
109662.e: In winter, lots of heavy snow lies on the trees and shrubs. Because of the snow pressure and creeping masses of snow, the trunks grow in a curve down the slope.
109662.m: Snow pressure bends the trunks in krummholz.

109663.q: Which two woody plants form most of the krummholz in the Swiss Alps?
a: Dwarf mountain pine and green alder
109663.e: Dwarf mountain pine often grows on limestone and dry slopes, green alder on damp, shady slopes. Both are very flexible.
109663.m: Dwarf mountain pine and green alder form most krummholz in the Alps.

109664.q: Why do green alder thickets often survive in avalanche paths?
a: The flexible branches spring back after the avalanche
109664.e: The springy trunks of the green alder lie flat under the snow. After the snow melts, they straighten up again.
109664.m: Flexible green alders survive even avalanches.

109665.q: What is the transition area between closed forest and the tree line called?
109665.e: In the battle zone, the forest has gaps and the trees are small and stunted. Here they fight to survive against cold, wind and snow.
109665.m: In the battle zone, trees fight against cold, wind and snow.

109666.q: What use are krummholz thickets on steep mountainsides?
a: They stop the soil from slipping
109666.e: The dense thickets hold the soil in place with their roots. They also slow down snow sliding down the slope.
109666.m: Krummholz holds the soil in place on steep slopes.

109667.q: Which tree with five needles per bundle often grows up to the tree line in the Alps?
109667.e: The Swiss stone pine has its needles in bundles of five. It can stand great cold and grows up to the tree line in the Engadine and Valais.
109667.m: The Swiss stone pine has five needles per bundle and grows up to the tree line.

109668.q: Why do many trees at the tree line grow almost without branches on the windy side?
a: Ice crystals in the wind grind the shoots away
Animals eat all the branches there
The trees drop them on purpose
109668.e: Strong wind drives ice crystals against the trees and dries out the shoots. Branches then only grow on the sheltered side; this is called flag growth.
109668.m: At the tree line, the wind shapes trees like flags.

109669.q: How does dwarf mountain pine grow on mountainsides?
a: With trunks that lie down and curve upwards
Dead straight with a single trunk
As a climbing plant on trees
109669.e: The trunks of dwarf mountain pine lie on the ground and grow upwards in a curve. This creates a dense thicket, often as tall as a person.
109669.m: Dwarf mountain pine grows with lying, curved trunks.

109670.q: How many needles does dwarf mountain pine have on a short shoot?
109670.e: Like other pines, dwarf mountain pine carries its needles in bundles. It has two needles per bundle.
109670.m: Dwarf mountain pine has two needles per bundle.

109672.q: Which tree genus does dwarf mountain pine belong to?
109672.e: Dwarf mountain pine is a form of the mountain pine.
109672.m: Dwarf mountain pine is a pine.

109673.q: Why is dwarf mountain pine hardly ever destroyed by snow and avalanches?
a: Its branches are flexible and lie flat
Its bark is made of stone
It drops all its branches in winter
109673.e: The springy branches of dwarf mountain pine bend under the weight of the snow. Avalanches slide over the flat thicket.
109673.m: Flexible branches protect dwarf mountain pine from snow damage.

109674.q: In which Swiss protected area do mountain pines make up a large part of the forest?
109674.e: In the Swiss National Park in the Engadine, mountain pines cover large areas, for example around the Ofen Pass. There are both upright forms and dwarf mountain pines there.
109674.m: Many mountain pines grow in the Swiss National Park.

109675.q: Where does dwarf mountain pine mainly grow in Switzerland?
a: In the mountains near the tree line
In the vineyards by the lake
On the Central Plateau between fields
In the marshes by the sea
109675.e: Dwarf mountain pine can stand cold, wind and lots of snow. That is why it grows mainly in the mountains, up to the tree line.
109675.m: Dwarf mountain pine grows in the mountains near the tree line.

109676.q: What protection do dense thickets of dwarf mountain pine give villages and roads in the valley?
a: They stop avalanches from breaking away
They keep floods in the sea
109676.e: The dense thicket holds the snow on the slope. This means fewer avalanches break away, and the soil is not washed away.
109676.m: Dwarf mountain pines help to stop avalanches on the slope.

109677.q: Why does the dandelion flower much later in the year on an alpine pasture than on the Central Plateau?
a: The snow melts later up there and it is cooler
The plants up there are a completely different species
The bees only come up there in autumn
The dandelion only flowers at night up there
109677.e: At high altitude, the warm season only begins after the snow melts. That is why the flowering time of the same plants moves later the higher you go.
109677.m: The higher up they grow, the later in the year plants flower.

109678.q: What often ends the growing season in the high mountains as early as September?
a: The end of the school holidays
109678.e: In the high mountains, frost and snow return early. After that, the plants rest until the next summer.
109678.m: Frost and snow end the summer early in the high mountains.

109679.q: Why is the water of glacier streams often milky and cloudy?
a: It is mixed with lime paint
109679.e: The glacier grinds rock into fine rock flour. This makes the meltwater cloudy; it is called glacier milk.
109679.m: Rock flour makes glacier water milky.

109680.q: What sometimes turns snowfields in the high mountains reddish in summer?
109680.e: Certain green algae live in the meltwater of the snow and produce a red protective pigment. This is called watermelon snow or blood snow.
109680.m: Red snow algae cause what is known as blood snow.

109681.q: Which yellow-flowered pioneer plant produces its flowers in spring even before its leaves?
109681.e: Coltsfoot quickly settles on bare ground, rubble and building sites. Its yellow flowers appear in spring, and the large leaves only follow later.
109681.m: Coltsfoot flowers before its leaves come out.

109782.q: What is the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye called?
109782.e: The retina lines the back of the inside of the eye. It contains the sensory cells that react to light.
109782.m: The retina is the light-sensitive layer in the eye.

109783.q: How does the image on the retina compare with the object being looked at?
109783.e: The cornea and lens work together like a converging lens in a camera and make an upside-down, smaller image. The brain processes it so that we see the world the right way up.
109783.m: The image on the retina is upside down.

109784.q: What do the sensory cells of the retina do with the light that falls on them?
a: They turn it into electrical signals
